The Relational Data Model and ER/EER-to-Relational Mapping

Chapters 5, 8 & 9 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.). Exercises 5.1–5.5, 5.11, 5.12, 5.15–5.17, 5.20, 9.2–9.8. Each topic below opens with its theory; the exercise topics give every assigned question with a full solution behind the Solution button. Questions marked must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

The story of this topic

This is where the Topic 3 diagram becomes tables. First, what a relation is, which constraints every valid state must satisfy, and how INSERT, DELETE and UPDATE can break them. Then the mapping algorithm, which turns each ER and EER construct into relations and foreign keys. Mapping answers are graded construct by construct, so name each step you apply and list every foreign key with what it references.

How the exercises are solved

Every assigned exercise, in textbook order. Each solution is written the way the Moodle keys are: assumptions with reasons, every step shown, and the final answer in an Answer box. Start with the exercises tagged ★ Must-do; they match past end-sem and quiz questions.

What is inside

    1  The relational model: concepts

    Theory recap

    The relational model (Codd, 1970) represents a database as a collection of relations. Informally a relation is a table of values: each row is a tuple representing a fact about an entity or relationship, each column header is an attribute naming the role its values play.

    Domains, attributes, tuples and relations

    Definition: Domain

    A domain DDD is a set of atomic values (indivisible as far as the model is concerned). It is specified by a name, a data type and a format, plus any information needed to interpret it (e.g. units). Examples: Usa_phone_numbers (10-digit strings (ddd)ddd-dddd), Grade_point_averages (reals in [0,4][0,4][0,4]), Employee_ages (integers 15 to 80), Academic_department_codes ({‘CS’, ‘ECON’, ‘PHYS’, …}).

    Definition: Relation schema, attribute, degree

    A relation schema R(A1,A2,…,An)R(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n)R(A1​,A2​,…,An​) is a relation name RRR plus a list of attributes AiA_iAi​. Each attribute AiA_iAi​ is the name of a role played by some domain DDD, written dom(Ai)\mathrm{dom}(A_i)dom(Ai​). The degree (arity) of the relation is nnn, the number of attributes. Example (degree 7): STUDENT(Name, Ssn, Home_phone, Address, Office_phone, Age, Gpa).

    Definition: Relation (relation state), tuple

    A relation or relation state r(R)r(R)r(R) is a set of nnn-tuples r={t1,…,tm}r=\{t_1,\dots,t_m\}r={t1​,…,tm​}. Each nnn-tuple is an ordered list of values t=⟨v1,…,vn⟩t=\langle v_1,\dots,v_n\ranglet=⟨v1​,…,vn​⟩ with each vi∈dom(Ai)v_i \in \mathrm{dom}(A_i)vi​∈dom(Ai​) or the special value NULL. Formally

    r(R)⊆dom(A1)×dom(A2)×⋯×dom(An),r(R) \subseteq \mathrm{dom}(A_1)\times \mathrm{dom}(A_2)\times\dots\times \mathrm{dom}(A_n),r(R)⊆dom(A1​)×dom(A2​)×⋯×dom(An​),

    so at most ∣dom(A1)∣×⋯×∣dom(An)∣|\mathrm{dom}(A_1)|\times\dots\times|\mathrm{dom}(A_n)|∣dom(A1​)∣×⋯×∣dom(An​)∣ tuples can ever exist; the current state holds only those that reflect the real world now. The number of tuples mmm is the relation’s cardinality.

    Several attributes can share a domain with different roles (Home_phone and Office_phone both have domain Usa_phone_numbers).

    Schema versus state

    Relation schema RRR (intension)Relation state r(R)r(R)r(R) (extension)
    What it isName + list of attributes (+ constraints)The set of tuples at a given moment
    Changes?Rarely (e.g. adding an attribute)Constantly: every insert/delete/update
    Database levelRelational database schema S={R1,…,Rm}S=\{R_1,\dots,R_m\}S={R1​,…,Rm​} plus a set of integrity constraints ICDatabase state DB={r1,…,rm}DB=\{r_1,\dots,r_m\}DB={r1​,…,rm​}, each rir_iri​ a state of RiR_iRi​, satisfying IC

    A database state that satisfies every constraint in IC is valid; otherwise it is not valid. The book avoids the word “instance” for a state, because “instance” is also used for a single tuple.

    Characteristics of relations

    • Tuples are not ordered. A relation is a set, and set elements have no order; a relation represents facts at a logical level, so any display order (by Name, by Ssn, …) shows the same relation. A file, by contrast, stores records in a physical order.
    • Values within a tuple are ordered under the first definition (attributes form a list). An alternative definition treats RRR as a set of attributes and each tuple as a mapping from attributes to values, i.e. a set of ⟨\langle⟨attribute, value⟩\rangle⟩ pairs (“self-describing data”); then attribute order does not matter either. The book uses the ordered definition for convenient notation.
    • Values are atomic (the flat relational model, the first normal form assumption): no composite or multivalued attributes. A composite attribute is stored as its simple components; a multivalued attribute needs a separate relation.
    • NULLs represent a value that is unknown, exists but is not available, or does not apply (undefined, e.g. the visa status of a domestic student). Two NULLs are not “equal” (two customers with NULL address need not share an address). Avoid NULLs in design where possible.
    • Interpretation. A schema is an assertion (“a student has a Name, Ssn, …”) and each tuple is a fact (an instance of the assertion). Relations can describe entities (STUDENT) or relationships (MAJORS(Student_ssn, Department_code)): the model represents both uniformly. Alternatively a schema is a predicate true for exactly the tuples in the state (closed world assumption: any fact not in the state is false).

    Notation

    • R(A1,…,An)R(A_1,\dots,A_n)R(A1​,…,An​): a relation schema of degree nnn. Q,R,SQ,R,SQ,R,S: relation names; q,r,sq,r,sq,r,s: relation states; t,u,vt,u,vt,u,v: tuples.
    • A bare relation name (STUDENT) denotes the current state; STUDENT(Name, Ssn, …) denotes the schema.
    • R.AR.AR.A qualifies an attribute (STUDENT.Name); attribute names are distinct within one relation.
    • t[Ai]t[A_i]t[Ai​] or t.Ait.A_it.Ai​ (or t[i]t[i]t[i]) is the value of AiA_iAi​ in ttt; t[Au,…,Az]t[A_u,\dots,A_z]t[Au​,…,Az​] is a subtuple. E.g. for Barbara Benson’s tuple, t[Ssn, Gpa, Age]=⟨t[\text{Ssn, Gpa, Age}] = \langlet[Ssn, Gpa, Age]=⟨‘533-69-1238’, 3.25, 19⟩\rangle⟩.

    2  Relational model constraints

    Theory recap

    Three categories of constraints

    CategoryMeaningExamples
    Inherent model-based (implicit)Follow from the definition of the model itselfNo duplicate tuples; atomic values; tuples unordered
    Schema-based (explicit)Expressed in the schema via the DDL; enforced by the DBMSDomain, key, NOT NULL, entity integrity, referential integrity
    Application-based (semantic constraints, business rules)Cannot be stated in the schema; enforced by application programs, or by SQL assertions/triggers“Salary ≤\le≤ supervisor’s salary”; “at most 56 hours per week over all projects”

    Data dependencies (functional and multivalued dependencies) are a further class, used to test design quality in normalization (Topic 5).

    Domain constraints

    Within each tuple, the value of each attribute AAA must be an atomic value from dom(A)\mathrm{dom}(A)dom(A) (or NULL if allowed). Domains are numeric types, characters, Booleans, fixed/variable-length strings, date/time/timestamp, subranges of a type, or enumerated sets.

    Key constraints: superkey, key, candidate key, primary key

    Definition: Superkey

    A set of attributes SK⊆RSK \subseteq RSK⊆R such that in every valid state r(R)r(R)r(R), for any two distinct tuples t1≠t2t_1 \neq t_2t1​=t2​: t1[SK]≠t2[SK]t_1[SK] \neq t_2[SK]t1​[SK]=t2​[SK] (a uniqueness constraint). Every relation has at least one superkey: the set of all its attributes (because tuples are distinct).

    Definition: Key (candidate key)

    A key KKK is a superkey that is minimal: removing any attribute from KKK leaves a set that is no longer a superkey. A key needs both uniqueness and minimality; a superkey needs only uniqueness. Every key is a superkey, not vice versa. A single-attribute superkey is always a key. If a schema has several keys, each is a candidate key.

    Definition: Primary key and unique keys

    One candidate key is designated the primary key (PK): its values identify tuples and are used in references from other relations. PK attributes are underlined. The other candidate keys are unique keys (not underlined; UNIQUE in SQL). Prefer a PK with a single or few attributes. Example: CAR(License_number, Engine_serial_number, Make, Model, Year) has candidate keys {License_number} and {Engine_serial_number}; the second is a unique key.

    Key idea

    A key is a property of the schema, determined by the meaning of the attributes, and must hold in every valid state (it is time-invariant). Name is not a key of STUDENT: two students could share a name, even if no two do today. For STUDENT, {Ssn} is a key and {Ssn, Name, Age} is a superkey but not a key (Name and Age can be dropped).

    Method: finding candidate keys from a given relation state

    Past papers give a small table and ask for the “smallest candidate key” or “primary key”.

    1. Test single attributes: a column with a repeated value is not a key (two tuples agree on it).
    2. Test pairs (then triples, …) built only from attributes, checking that no two rows agree on all of them.
    3. Keep only the minimal unique sets: a set is discarded if a proper subset is already unique.
    4. State the caveat: data can only refute a key. A set unique in this state is only a candidate for a key; whether it is a key depends on the meaning (state the assumption).
    Worked example: keys from data

    ENROL(Roll, Name, Course, Slot, Grade), current state:

    RollNameCourseSlotGrade
    1AshaDBMonA
    1AshaOSTueB
    2RaviDBMonA
    3AshaDBWedC
    2RaviCNTueA

    Singles: Roll repeats (1), Name repeats (Asha), Course repeats (DB), Slot repeats (Mon), Grade repeats (A): no single attribute is a key.
    Pairs: {Roll, Course}: (1,DB),(1,OS),(2,DB),(3,DB),(2,CN) all distinct, so unique. {Roll, Slot}: (1,Mon),(1,Tue),(2,Mon),(3,Wed),(2,Tue) distinct, unique. {Name, Slot}: distinct, unique. {Name, Course}: (Asha,DB) appears twice, not unique. {Roll, Name}: (1,Asha) twice, not unique.
    Triples: the only new minimal one is {Name, Course, Grade}.
    Minimal unique sets in this state (checked by program over all 31 subsets): {Roll, Course}, {Roll, Slot}, {Name, Slot}, {Name, Course, Grade}.
    Semantics: names repeat in general and a grade does not identify anything, so {Name, Slot} and {Name, Course, Grade} are coincidences of this state. A student takes a course once, so {Roll, Course} is the natural primary key (smallest size, 2 attributes). If a student can attend only one class per slot, {Roll, Slot} is a second candidate key (a unique key).

    Method: counting superkeys

    Every superset of a candidate key is a superkey. With nnn attributes:

    • one candidate key of kkk attributes: the other n−kn-kn−k attributes may be in or out, so 2 n−k2^{\,n-k}2n−k superkeys;
    • several candidate keys K1,K2,…K_1,K_2,\dotsK1​,K2​,…: use inclusion–exclusion on “contains KiK_iKi​”: ∣S1∪S2∣=2n−∣K1∣+2n−∣K2∣−2n−∣K1∪K2∣|S_1\cup S_2| = 2^{n-|K_1|} + 2^{n-|K_2|} - 2^{n-|K_1\cup K_2|}∣S1​∪S2​∣=2n−∣K1​∣+2n−∣K2​∣−2n−∣K1​∪K2​∣;
    • kkk single-attribute candidate keys (e.g. three unique attributes): (2k−1)⋅2 n−k(2^k-1)\cdot 2^{\,n-k}(2k−1)⋅2n−k (each non-empty choice of key attributes, times anything for the rest).

    Constraints on NULL values

    A NOT NULL constraint forbids NULL in an attribute (e.g. every STUDENT must have a Name). PK attributes are implicitly NOT NULL (entity integrity, below).

    Entity integrity, referential integrity and foreign keys

    Definition: Entity integrity constraint

    No primary key value can be NULL (not even part of a composite PK). The PK identifies tuples; with NULL keys we could not tell tuples apart or reference them.

    Key and entity integrity constraints are on single relations. Referential integrity is between two relations (or a relation and itself): a tuple that refers to another relation must refer to an existing tuple.

    Definition: Foreign key (and referential integrity)

    A set of attributes FKFKFK of R1R_1R1​ is a foreign key of R1R_1R1​ that references R2R_2R2​ if

    1. the attributes of FKFKFK have the same domain(s) as the primary key PKPKPK of R2R_2R2​; and
    2. for every tuple t1t_1t1​ of r1(R1)r_1(R_1)r1​(R1​), either t1[FK]=t2[PK]t_1[FK] = t_2[PK]t1​[FK]=t2​[PK] for some tuple t2t_2t2​ of r2(R2)r_2(R_2)r2​(R2​) (“t1t_1t1​ references t2t_2t2​”), or t1[FK]t_1[FK]t1​[FK] is NULL.

    R1R_1R1​ is the referencing relation, R2R_2R2​ the referenced relation. We write Dno → DEPARTMENT.Dnumber and draw an arrow from the FK to the referenced PK.

    • A FK may reference its own relation: EMPLOYEE.Super_ssn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn.
    • A FK may be NULL (employee not yet assigned to a department) unless declared NOT NULL; but if it is part of the referencing relation’s PK it can never be NULL (entity integrity).
    • A composite FK references the whole composite PK, never part of it.
    • FKs can have a different name from the PK they reference (Dno, Dnum, Dnumber all mean a department number); conversely, the same concept used in two roles in one relation needs two names (Ssn, Super_ssn).

    Other constraints: semantic, state and transition

    • Semantic integrity constraints (business rules) are not part of the basic DDL: “salary of an employee ≤\le≤ salary of the supervisor”, “max 56 hours per week on all projects”. Enforced in application programs, or with SQL CREATE ASSERTION / CREATE TRIGGER (Topic 8).
    • State (static) constraints restrict what a valid state looks like (all of the above).
    • Transition (dynamic) constraints restrict how the state may change: “salary can only increase”. Enforced by application programs or active rules/triggers.

    3  Update operations and dealing with constraint violations

    Theory recap

    The three update operations are Insert (new tuples), Delete (tuples chosen by a condition) and Update/Modify (change attribute values of chosen tuples). Every operation must leave the database in a valid state. This section covers domain, key, entity integrity and referential integrity constraints (the book’s scope, Figure 5.7).

    Insert: can violate all four

    • Domain: a value not in the attribute’s domain or of the wrong type.
    • Key: the new tuple’s key value already exists in another tuple.
    • Entity integrity: any part of the new tuple’s PK is NULL.
    • Referential integrity: a FK value in the new tuple refers to a tuple that does not exist in the referenced relation (and is not NULL).
    Book examples on the Figure 5.6 state
    Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘Cecilia’, ‘F’, ‘Kolonsky’, NULL, ‘1960-04-05’, ‘6357 Windy Lane, Katy, TX’, F, 28000, NULL, 4⟩\rangle⟩ into EMPLOYEEEntity integrity (PK Ssn NULL): rejected.
    Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘Alicia’, ‘J’, ‘Zelaya’, ‘999887777’, …, ‘987654321’, 4⟩\rangle⟩Key constraint (Ssn exists): rejected.
    Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘Cecilia’, …, ‘677678989’, …, ‘987654321’, 7⟩\rangle⟩RI on Dno (no department 7).
    Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘Cecilia’, …, ‘677678989’, …, NULL, 4⟩\rangle⟩Satisfies all: accepted.

    Options on violation: the default is to reject the insertion (ideally with the reason). Alternatively the DBMS can try to correct the cause: ask for a valid Ssn; for an RI violation ask the user to change Dno to a valid value or NULL, or to first insert the referenced DEPARTMENT tuple (which may itself cascade, e.g. if its Mgr_ssn does not exist).

    Delete: can violate only referential integrity

    Deleting tuple ttt violates RI if ttt is referenced by FK values of other tuples. It cannot violate domain, key or entity integrity (deleting never creates a value).

    • Delete WORKS_ON tuple (999887777, 10): acceptable (nothing references WORKS_ON).
    • Delete EMPLOYEE 999887777: referenced by WORKS_ON tuples: violation.
    • Delete EMPLOYEE 333445555: referenced from four relations: EMPLOYEE (Super_ssn), DEPARTMENT (Mgr_ssn), WORKS_ON and DEPENDENT.

    Options on violation:

    1. Restrict (reject, NO ACTION/RESTRICT): refuse the deletion.
    2. Cascade: also delete the referencing tuples (e.g. the WORKS_ON and DEPENDENT tuples of the deleted employee).
    3. Set null: set the referencing FK values to NULL; impossible if the FK is part of the referencing relation’s PK (entity integrity), e.g. WORKS_ON.Essn.
    4. Set default: set the referencing FK values to a default valid value.

    Combinations are common: cascade into WORKS_ON/DEPENDENT, but set Super_ssn/Mgr_ssn to NULL or another valid employee (deleting other employees or a department would be wrong).

    Update: depends on which attribute changes

    • Neither PK nor FK: only the domain (and NOT NULL) needs checking. Update Salary of 999887777 to 28000: acceptable.
    • FK attribute: the new value must exist in the referenced relation or be NULL (RI, referencing side). Dno of 999887777 to 1: acceptable; to 7: RI violation.
    • PK attribute: like a delete followed by an insert, so key (new value duplicates), entity integrity (new value NULL) and RI (old value is referenced elsewhere) can all be violated. Ssn of 999887777 to 987654321: key violation and RI violation (tuples referencing 999887777).

    Options: for the referencing side, reject (or correct); for the referenced side (PK changed), the same options as Delete, chosen separately: ON UPDATE CASCADE / SET NULL / SET DEFAULT / RESTRICT.

    Delete–––✓ (deleted tuple is referenced)Restrict/reject; cascade; set null; set default (or a combination)

    Declaring the options in SQL DDL (see Topic 8)
    CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE ( ...,
  Dno INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  CONSTRAINT EMPPK  PRIMARY KEY (Ssn),
  CONSTRAINT EMPSUPERFK FOREIGN KEY (Super_ssn) REFERENCES EMPLOYEE(Ssn)
      ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT EMPDEPTFK  FOREIGN KEY (Dno) REFERENCES DEPARTMENT(Dnumber)
      ON DELETE SET DEFAULT ON UPDATE CASCADE );
    Common mistakes
    • Saying a Delete can violate a key or entity integrity constraint. It can only break RI.
    • Saying an Insert into a relation with no foreign keys (e.g. SALESPERSON) can violate RI. RI is violated by an Insert only on the referencing side.
    • Offering “set null” for a FK that is part of the PK (WORKS_ON.Essn, DEPENDENT.Essn).
    • Forgetting that a NULL FK is allowed (unless NOT NULL is declared): inserting an employee with Super_ssn = NULL is fine.
    • Listing only the first violation: the question says “all integrity constraints violated”. An insert can violate key and RI at once (Exercise 5.11(c)).

    Transactions

    A transaction is an executing program containing database operations (retrievals, inserts, deletes, updates) that together form an atomic unit of work; at its end the database must be in a valid, consistent state. It differs from a single update operation because it may group many operations, and intermediate states inside it may temporarily violate constraints (e.g. a bank withdrawal reads the balance, checks it, then updates it).

    Past-paper pattern 1: which constraints does each operation violate?

    4  Relational query languages · Chapter 8, in brief

    Theory recap

    The model has two formal query languages, both operating on relations and producing relations:

    • Relational algebra (procedural): a set of operations (σ\sigmaσ select, π\piπ project, ρ\rhoρ rename, ∪\cup∪, ∩\cap∩, −-−, ×\times×, joins ⋈\bowtie⋈, division ÷\div÷, aggregation I\mathfrak{I}I, outer joins) composed into expressions that say how to compute the answer. It underlies query processing and optimization in RDBMSs. Example: πFname, Lname(σDno=5(EMPLOYEE))\pi_{\text{Fname, Lname}}\left(\sigma_{\text{Dno=5}}\left(EMPLOYEE\right)\right)πFname, Lname​(σDno=5​(EMPLOYEE)).
    • Relational calculus (declarative): tuple relational calculus (TRC) describes what the answer is with a formula, e.g. { t.Fname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Dno=5 }\{\,t.\mathit{Fname} \mid \mathit{EMPLOYEE}(t) \mathbin{\textbf{and}} t.\mathit{Dno}=5\,\}{t.Fname∣EMPLOYEE(t)andt.Dno=5}. A language that can express every query of the basic relational algebra is relationally complete; SQL is based on TRC.

    The joins in these languages are how a relational schema materializes relationships: an FK–PK equijoin rebuilds each binary relationship (Section 5.4). Details and exercises: Topic 6 (relational algebra) and Topic 7 (tuple relational calculus).

    5  ER-to-relational mapping · Chapter 9.1

    Theory recap

    The mapping algorithm turns a conceptual ER schema into a relational schema with primary keys, unique keys and referential integrity constraints. The running example is the COMPANY ER schema (Figure 9.1).

    The COMPANY ER schema (Figure 9.1)

    The algorithm, Steps 1–7

    Definition: Step 1: regular (strong) entity types

    For each regular entity type EEE create a relation RRR with all simple attributes of EEE (only the simple components of a composite attribute). Choose one key of EEE as the PK of RRR (a composite key’s components together form the PK). Record the other keys as unique keys. Derived attributes are not stored (or are clearly marked as derived). FKs and relationship attributes are added in later steps.

    COMPANY: EMPLOYEE(Fname, Minit, Lname, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Sex, Salary), DEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber) (Dname UNIQUE), PROJECT(Pname, Pnumber, Plocation) (Pname UNIQUE). Name is composite, so only Fname, Minit, Lname are stored; Number_of_employees is derived (a COUNT), not stored. Such relations are called entity relations.

    Definition: Step 2: weak entity types

    For each weak entity type WWW with owner EEE, create RRR with the simple attributes of WWW and, as a FK, the PK of the owner’s relation. PK(R)(R)(R) = owner’s PK ∪\cup∪ partial key of WWW. This maps the identifying relationship (no extra relation). If the owner is itself weak, map the owner first. Use ON DELETE/UPDATE CASCADE on this FK (existence dependency).

    COMPANY: DEPENDENT(Essn, Dependent_name, Sex, Bdate, Relationship), Essn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn.

    Definition: Step 3: binary 1:1 relationship types (three options)

    Let SSS and TTT be the relations of the participants.

    1. Foreign key approach (preferred): put the PK of TTT as a FK in SSS, choosing for SSS an entity type with total participation; add the relationship’s simple attributes to SSS. The FK is UNIQUE (1:1) and, if participation of SSS is total, NOT NULL.
    2. Merged relation: merge both entity types and the relationship into one relation; appropriate when both participations are total (both tables always have the same number of tuples).
    3. Cross-reference (relationship relation): a third relation RRR holding the PKs of SSS and TTT as FKs; PK(R)(R)(R) = one of them, the other is a unique key. Costs an extra relation and joins; useful when few entities participate (avoids NULL FKs).

    COMPANY: MANAGES, DEPARTMENT participates totally, so add Mgr_ssn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn (NOT NULL, UNIQUE) and Mgr_start_date (from Start_date) to DEPARTMENT. The reverse choice (a Department_managed FK in EMPLOYEE) would be NULL for the  98% of employees who manage nothing.

    Definition: Step 4: binary 1:N relationship types

    Foreign key approach (preferred): in the relation SSS on the N-side, add as FK the PK of the relation TTT on the 1-side (each N-side entity relates to at most one 1-side entity); add the relationship’s simple attributes to SSS. NOT NULL if the N-side participation is total. Relationship-relation approach (alternative): a relation with both PKs; its PK is the N-side’s PK. Use when few N-side tuples participate (avoids many NULLs).

    COMPANY: WORKS_FOR gives Dno → DEPARTMENT.Dnumber in EMPLOYEE; SUPERVISION (recursive) gives Super_ssn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn in EMPLOYEE; CONTROLS gives Dnum → DEPARTMENT.Dnumber in PROJECT.

    Definition: Step 5: binary M:N relationship types

    The only option (in the basic, 1NF model): a new relationship relation SSS with the PKs of both participants as FKs; their combination is PK(S)(S)(S). Add the relationship’s simple attributes. Use CASCADE on both FKs (each relationship instance depends on both entities).

    COMPANY: WORKS_ON(Essn, Pno, Hours), Essn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn, Pno → PROJECT.Pnumber.

    Definition: Step 6: multivalued attributes

    For each multivalued attribute AAA, create a relation RRR with an attribute for AAA plus the PK KKK of the relation of the entity (or relationship) type owning AAA, as a FK. PK(R)={A,K}(R) = \{A, K\}(R)={A,K}. If AAA is composite, include its simple components (and decide which of them belong in the key). CASCADE on the FK.

    COMPANY: DEPT_LOCATIONS(Dnumber, Dlocation), Dnumber → DEPARTMENT.Dnumber.

    Definition: Step 7: n-ary relationship types (n>2n>2n>2)

    Create a relationship relation SSS with the PKs of all nnn participants as FKs plus the simple attributes of the relationship. PK(S)(S)(S) is usually the combination of all the FKs, but if a participant EEE has cardinality 1 in the relationship, the FK to EEE is not part of the PK (it is determined by the others).

    Example: ternary SUPPLY(SUPPLIER, PART, PROJECT) gives SUPPLY(Sname, Proj_name, Part_no, Quantity) with three FKs.

    The complete COMPANY mapping

    StepER constructRelational result
    1EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT, PROJECTEMPLOYEE(Fname, Minit, Lname, Ssn, Bdate, Address, Sex, Salary); DEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber); PROJECT(Pname, Pnumber, Plocation); Dname, Pname UNIQUE; Name split into components; Number_of_employees not stored
    2weak DEPENDENT, DEPENDENTS_OFDEPENDENT(Essn, Dependent_name, Sex, Bdate, Relationship); Essn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn
    3MANAGES (1:1, DEPARTMENT total)add Mgr_ssn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn (NOT NULL, UNIQUE), Mgr_start_date to DEPARTMENT
    4WORKS_FOR, SUPERVISION, CONTROLS (1:N)EMPLOYEE: Dno → DEPARTMENT.Dnumber (NOT NULL: total), Super_ssn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn; PROJECT: Dnum → DEPARTMENT.Dnumber (NOT NULL: total)
    5WORKS_ON (M:N)WORKS_ON(Essn, Pno, Hours)
    6multivalued LocationsDEPT_LOCATIONS(Dnumber, Dlocation)
    7(no n-ary relationships)–

    The result is exactly the schema of Figure 5.7 drawn above.

    What the mapping cannot enforce

    Some ER constraints have no FK equivalent: total participation of the 1-side or of an M:N participant (“every department has at least one employee”, “every employee works on some project”), or (min,max) bounds such as “at most 4 projects”. State them as constraints to be enforced by assertions/triggers or the application; do not drop them silently.

    Correspondence between ER and relational models (Table 9.1)

    ER modelRelational model
    Entity typeEntity relation
    1:1 or 1:N relationship typeForeign key (or relationship relation)
    M:N relationship typeRelationship relation and two foreign keys
    nnn-ary relationship typeRelationship relation and nnn foreign keys
    Simple attributeAttribute
    Composite attributeSet of simple component attributes
    Multivalued attributeRelation and foreign key
    Value setDomain
    Key attributePrimary (or secondary/unique) key
    Weak entity type (extra row, Step 2)Relation whose PK = owner PK + partial key; FK to owner

    Relationships are not explicit in a relational schema: they are FK–PK pairs over the same domain. Related tuples are combined with an equijoin on FK = PK: one join for a 1:1/1:N FK mapping, two joins for an M:N relationship relation, nnn joins for an nnn-ary one. E.g. employee name, project name, hours: EMPLOYEE⋈Ssn=EssnWORKS_ON⋈Pno=PnumberPROJECT\textsf{EMPLOYEE} \mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{Ssn=Essn}}} \textsf{WORKS\_ON} \mathbin{\bowtie_{\text{Pno=Pnumber}}} \textsf{PROJECT}EMPLOYEE⋈Ssn=Essn​WORKS_ON⋈Pno=Pnumber​PROJECT. Joining on attributes that are not an FK–PK pair (e.g. Plocation = Dlocation) gives meaningless, spurious tuples.

    Theory recap

    Step 8: specialization / generalization

    Specialization with superclass CCC (attributes {k,a1,…,an}\{k, a_1,\dots,a_n\}{k,a1​,…,an​}, PK kkk) and subclasses S1,…,SmS_1,\dots,S_mS1​,…,Sm​. Attrs(R)\mathrm{Attrs}(R)Attrs(R) = attributes, PK(R)\mathrm{PK}(R)PK(R) = primary key.

Works for every specialization: total or partial, disjoint or overlapping. Retrieving all attributes of an SiS_iSi​ entity needs an equijoin Li⋈LL_i \bowtie LLi​⋈L.

    Definition: Option 8B: multiple relations, subclass relations only

    For each subclass Li(k,a1,…,an,attributes of Si)L_i(k, a_1,\dots,a_n, \text{attributes of } S_i)Li​(k,a1​,…,an​,attributes of Si​) with PK kkk; no relation for CCC. Only for total specializations (otherwise entities in no subclass are lost) and recommended only if disjoint (if overlapping, an entity’s inherited attributes are stored redundantly in several LiL_iLi​). Listing all of CCC needs an OUTER UNION of the LiL_iLi​; other relations cannot have a single FK to “CCC”.

    Definition: Option 8C: single relation with one type attribute

    L(k,a1,…,an,attrs of S1,…,attrs of Sm,t)L(k, a_1,\dots,a_n, \text{attrs of } S_1,\dots,\text{attrs of } S_m, t)L(k,a1​,…,an​,attrs of S1​,…,attrs of Sm​,t) with PK kkk, where the type (discriminating) attribute ttt says which subclass a tuple belongs to (domain {1,…,m}\{1,\dots,m\}{1,…,m}; NULL if partial and in no subclass; NOT NULL enforces totality). Only for disjoint specializations. If attribute-defined, the defining attribute is ttt. Many NULLs if subclasses have many local attributes.

    Definition: Option 8D: single relation with multiple type attributes

    L(k,a1,…,an,attrs of all Si,t1,…,tm)L(k, a_1,\dots,a_n, \text{attrs of all } S_i, t_1,\dots,t_m)L(k,a1​,…,an​,attrs of all Si​,t1​,…,tm​) with PK kkk, each tit_iti​ a Boolean flag “belongs to SiS_iSi​”. Designed for overlapping specializations (also works for disjoint ones). Same NULL drawback as 8C.

    OptionPartialTotalDisjointOverlapUse when / drawback
    8A super + subs✓✓✓✓Always valid; subclasses with many own attributes or own relationships. Needs joins.
    8B subs only–✓✓(redundant)Total and disjoint; no relation references the superclass as a whole.

    Figure 9.5: the four options

    8A for EMPLOYEE/{SECRETARY, TECHNICIAN, ENGINEER}: EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Fname, Minit, Lname, Birth_date, Address, Job_type), SECRETARY(Ssn, Typing_speed), TECHNICIAN(Ssn, Tgrade), ENGINEER(Ssn, Eng_type) (each Ssn → EMPLOYEE.Ssn).
    8B for VEHICLE/{CAR, TRUCK} (total, disjoint): CAR(Vehicle_id, License_plate_no, Price, Max_speed, No_of_passengers), TRUCK(Vehicle_id, License_plate_no, Price, No_of_axles, Tonnage).

    Multilevel hierarchies and lattices may mix options (Figure 9.6: 8A for PERSON/{EMPLOYEE, ALUMNUS, STUDENT}, 8C inside EMPLOYEE with Employee_type, 8D flags for STUDENT_ASSISTANT). Shared subclasses (multiple inheritance, all superclasses with the same key) can use any option allowed by Step 8.

    Step 9: categories (union types)

    Definition: Step 9: mapping a category

    If the defining superclasses have different keys, create a relation for the category with a new surrogate key (e.g. Owner_id) as its PK, plus the category’s own attributes; add the surrogate key as a FK in each superclass relation (NULL for superclass entities not in the category; UNIQUE). A type attribute in the category relation (which superclass a tuple comes from) is recommended. If the superclasses share the same key, no surrogate is needed: use that key.

    Figure 9.7: OWNER = PERSON ∪\cup∪ BANK ∪\cup∪ COMPANY

    PERSON(Ssn, Driver_license_no, Name, Address, Owner_id), BANK(Bname, Baddress, Owner_id), COMPANY(Cname, Caddress, Owner_id), OWNER(Owner_id); each Owner_id → OWNER.Owner_id. REGISTERED_VEHICLE = CAR ∪\cup∪ TRUCK share the key Vehicle_id: REGISTERED_VEHICLE(Vehicle_id, License_plate_number), CAR(Vehicle_id, Cstyle, Cmake, Cmodel, Cyear), TRUCK(Vehicle_id, Tmake, Tmodel, Tonnage, Tyear), OWNS(Owner_id, Vehicle_id, Purchase_date, Lien_or_regular).

    7  How mapping answers are graded

    Theory recap

    From the course’s EtoR rubrics (individual assignment EtoR-I and Group Assignment 3). A complete answer has (1) every relation with its attributes and PK underlined, (2) a schema diagram with an arrow from each FK to the PK it references, (3) a short explanation of how each construct was mapped, and the assumptions.

    Major mistakesEtoR-IGA3
    A relation has no PK, or a (regular) entity type is not mappedM1M1
    A weak entity’s PK does not include its owner’s full keyM2M2
    A FK references only part of a composite keyM3M3
    A 1:N relationship is not mapped, or its FK is on the wrong (1-) sideM4M4
    An M:N relationship is not a separate relation, or its PK lacks a participant’s keyM5M5
    A ternary relationship mapped as binary, not a separate relation, or PK lacks a required participant–M6
    A multivalued attribute kept as a column of its entity’s relationM6M7
    A relationship attribute placed in the wrong relationM7–
    Specialization not mapped, or mapped so its constraints are lost (e.g. 8C for an overlapping one)M8M8
    Some relationship (diamond) not mapped at all, neither as relation nor as FK–M9
    No FK arrows drawn at allM9M10
    Minor mistakes
    One FK arrow missing or reversedm1m1
    One PK attribute not underlined (key still clear)m2m2
    Composite attribute kept as a single attributem3m3
    Derived attribute stored without being marked derivedm4m4
    Identifying relationship mapped as an extra relation / foldable relationship made a relation without assumptionm5m5
    No NOT NULL on a FK that carries total participationm6m6
    No UNIQUE on a FK folded in from a 1:1 relationship–m7
    An attribute of the diagram’s own entities missing–m8
    Explanation or assumptions missingm7m9

    Grades: A = no major and at most 2 minor; B = 1 major or ≥3\ge 3≥3 minor; C = 2–3 major (bare-bones); D = ≥4\ge 4≥4 major or largely missing. Each occurrence counts (the same mistake in NNN places is NNN mistakes), but one wrong key carried consistently is counted once. A valid alternative with a stated, justified assumption is accepted (surrogate keys, 8B/8D where valid, a relationship attribute in the key); an unstated one costs a minor mistake. Attribute names do not matter; structure does. One arrow per FK group or per attribute are both fine.

    Answer template for any mapping question
    1. Assumptions A1, A2, … with a why (keys chosen, how a ternary’s 1s are read, which Step 8 option and why).
    2. Go step by step: Step 1 … Step 9, naming the construct handled in each.
    3. Final schema: one line per relation, PK underlined, then every FK as A → R.B, with NOT NULL for total participation and UNIQUE for 1:1 FKs; composite FKs written as a group: (Title, Year) → TV_SHOW.
    4. A schema diagram with an arrow from every FK to its PK.
    5. A sentence on constraints the schema cannot enforce (min >>> 1, total participation on the 1-side).
    How the Moodle key writes it (EtoR-I, TV shows)

    TV_SHOW(Title, Year, Company_Name), Company_Name → PRODUCTION_COMPANY (NOT NULL); SEASON(Title, Year, Season_No), (Title, Year) → TV_SHOW; EPISODE(Title, Year, Season_No, Episode_No, Duration_Min, Plot_Outline), (Title, Year, Season_No) → SEASON (owner SEASON is itself weak, so EPISODE carries its full three-part key); multivalued Genre becomes TV_SHOW_GENRE(Title, Year, Genre); overlapping total PERSON/{DIRECTOR, ACTOR} uses 8A (8B or 8D accepted with a stated assumption; 8C not accepted, it cannot represent a person who both acts and directs); derived counts are not stored.

    8  Chapter 5 exercises

    Textbook exercises

    5.1Relational-model termsE&N Ex. 5.1 · p. 170

    Define the following terms as they apply to the relational model of data: domain, attribute, nnn-tuple, relation schema, relation state, degree of a relation, relational database schema, and relational database state.

    Solution · written for this guide
    TermDefinition (with COMPANY / STUDENT example)
    DomainA named set of atomic values with a data type and format, e.g. Social_security_numbers = valid 9-digit strings.
    AttributeThe name of the role a domain plays in a relation schema; dom(A)\mathrm{dom}(A)dom(A) is its domain. Ssn and Super_ssn are two attributes over the same domain.
    nnn-tupleAn ordered list ⟨v1,…,vn⟩\langle v_1,\dots,v_n\rangle⟨v1​,…,vn​⟩ of values, each vi∈dom(Ai)v_i\in\mathrm{dom}(A_i)vi​∈dom(Ai​) or NULL; one row, e.g. the EMPLOYEE tuple of John Smith.
    Relation schemaR(A1,…,An)R(A_1,\dots,A_n)R(A1​,…,An​): a relation name and a list of attributes, e.g. DEPARTMENT(Dname, Dnumber, Mgr_ssn, Mgr_start_date).
    Relation stater(R)r(R)r(R): a set of nnn-tuples of RRR at a given time, r(R)⊆dom(A1)×⋯×dom(An)r(R)\subseteq\mathrm{dom}(A_1)\times\dots\times\mathrm{dom}(A_n)r(R)⊆dom(A1​)×⋯×dom(An​); e.g. the 3 DEPARTMENT tuples of Figure 5.6.
    Degree (arity)The number nnn of attributes of the schema; EMPLOYEE has degree 10.
    Relational database schemaS={R1,…,Rm}S=\{R_1,\dots,R_m\}S={R1​,…,Rm​} plus a set of integrity constraints IC; e.g. COMPANY = {EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT, DEPT_LOCATIONS, PROJECT, WORKS_ON, DEPENDENT}.
    Relational database stateDB={r1,…,rm}DB=\{r_1,\dots,r_m\}DB={r1​,…,rm​}, a state rir_iri​ of each RiR_iRi​, satisfying IC (a valid state); e.g. Figure 5.6.
    5.2Why tuples are unorderedE&N Ex. 5.2 · p. 170

    Why are tuples in a relation not ordered?

    Solution · written for this guide

    A relation is defined as a set of tuples, and the elements of a mathematical set have no order. The relation represents facts at a logical level, and the meaning of a fact does not depend on its position: the STUDENT relation sorted by Name and the same relation sorted by Age (Figures 5.1, 5.2) are the same relation. Ordering is a property of the physical storage (a file stores records in some order) or of a particular display/query result (ORDER BY), not of the relation. Keeping order out of the model also lets the DBMS store tuples in whatever order is efficient (data independence).

    Answer

    Because a relation is a set of tuples (sets are unordered) describing facts logically; any order is a storage or presentation choice, and all orderings denote the same relation.

    5.3Why duplicate tuples are not allowedE&N Ex. 5.3 · p. 170

    Why are duplicate tuples not allowed in a relation?

    Solution · written for this guide
    • By definition a relation is a set, and a set cannot contain the same element twice.
    • Each tuple asserts one fact; asserting it twice adds no information (“Smith works on project 1 for 32.5 hours” stated twice is still one fact) and would only create redundancy and update problems (which copy to change or delete?).
    • Distinctness guarantees that every relation has a superkey (at least the set of all attributes) and hence a key, so every tuple can be identified and referenced by foreign keys.

    (SQL tables are multisets and can hold duplicates unless a PRIMARY KEY/UNIQUE constraint is declared; the formal relational model does not allow them.)

    5.4Key vs. superkeyE&N Ex. 5.4 · p. 170★ Must-do

    What is the difference between a key and a superkey?

    Solution · written for this guide
    SuperkeyKey (candidate key)
    DefinitionA set SKSKSK of attributes such that no two distinct tuples in any valid state have the same SKSKSK value: t1[SK]≠t2[SK]t_1[SK]\neq t_2[SK]t1​[SK]=t2​[SK]A superkey KKK that is minimal: removing any attribute from KKK gives a set that is no longer a superkey
    UniquenessYesYes
    MinimalityNot required (may contain redundant attributes)Required
    How manyMany: every superset of a key; at least one (all attributes)Usually few; one is chosen as the primary key
    Example (STUDENT){Ssn}, {Ssn, Name}, {Ssn, Name, Age}, …{Ssn} only

    A single-attribute superkey is always a key. {Ssn, Name, Age} is a superkey but not a key, because Name and Age can be removed and uniqueness still holds. Both are properties of the schema: they must hold in every valid state and are decided by meaning, not by one state.

    Counting (as asked in quizzes): with nnn attributes and a single-attribute key, there are 2n−12^{n-1}2n−1 superkeys; STUDENT (7 attributes, key Ssn) has 26=642^6=6426=64 superkeys and 1 key. With several keys use inclusion–exclusion (theory, Section on counting superkeys).

    Answer

    A superkey only has to be unique; a key is a superkey that is also minimal (no attribute can be dropped). Every key is a superkey; not every superkey is a key.

    What the grader checks

    Full marks need both properties named (uniqueness, minimality) and an example of a superkey that is not a key. “Key = primary key” is a common wrong answer: a relation can have several candidate keys.

    5.5Why designate a primary keyE&N Ex. 5.5 · p. 170

    Why do we designate one of the candidate keys of a relation to be the primary key?

    Solution · written for this guide
    • Tuples need one agreed identifier: the value other relations store as a foreign key to reference the tuple (DEPARTMENT is referenced by Dnumber, not by Dname), so references are uniform.
    • Entity integrity is enforced on it (no NULLs), guaranteeing every tuple is identifiable.
    • The DBMS usually builds its primary index / storage organization on it, so lookups and joins use it.

    The choice among candidate keys is somewhat arbitrary; prefer a single or few attributes, stable (rarely changing) and never NULL. The others become unique keys (UNIQUE), still enforced but not used for references. Example: CAR has candidate keys License_number and Engine_serial_number; one is chosen as PK, the other declared UNIQUE.

    5.11Constraint violations on the COMPANY stateE&N Ex. 5.11 · p. 170★ Must-do

    Suppose that each of the following Update operations is applied directly to the database state shown in Figure 5.6. Discuss all integrity constraints violated by each operation, if any, and the different ways of enforcing these constraints.

    1. Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘Robert’, ‘F’, ‘Scott’, ‘943775543’, ‘1972-06-21’, ‘2365 Newcastle Rd, Bellaire, TX’, M, 58000, ‘888665555’, 1⟩\rangle⟩ into EMPLOYEE.
    2. Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘ProductA’, 4, ‘Bellaire’, 2⟩\rangle⟩ into PROJECT.
    3. Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘Production’, 4, ‘943775543’, ‘2007-10-01’⟩\rangle⟩ into DEPARTMENT.
    4. Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘677678989’, NULL, ‘40.0’⟩\rangle⟩ into WORKS_ON.
    5. Insert ⟨\langle⟨‘453453453’, ‘John’, ‘M’, ‘1990-12-12’, ‘spouse’⟩\rangle⟩ into DEPENDENT.
    6. Delete the WORKS_ON tuples with Essn = ‘333445555’.
    7. Delete the EMPLOYEE tuple with Ssn = ‘987654321’.
    8. Delete the PROJECT tuple with Pname = ‘ProductX’.
    9. Modify the Mgr_ssn and Mgr_start_date of the DEPARTMENT tuple with Dnumber = 5 to ‘123456789’ and ‘2007-10-01’, respectively.
    10. Modify the Super_ssn attribute of the EMPLOYEE tuple with Ssn = ‘999887777’ to ‘943775543’.
    11. Modify the Hours attribute of the WORKS_ON tuple with Essn = ‘999887777’ and Pno = 10 to ‘5.0’.

    (The Figure 5.6 state and the Figure 5.7 constraints are reproduced in the theory part.)

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Constraints considered: domain, key (PKs of Figure 5.7, plus the unique keys Dname and Pname), entity integrity and the eight referential integrity constraints of Figure 5.7. Why: these are the constraints the book declares on COMPANY (Section 5.3).
    2. Each operation is applied to the original Figure 5.6 state, not after the previous ones (the question says “directly”). So in (c) and (j) employee 943775543 does not exist, even though (a) would insert him.
    3. Values such as ‘40.0’ (quoted) and M (unquoted) are read as the intended number/character, not as domain errors. Why: the book’s notation is informal about quotes.

    The violations below were checked on an SQLite copy of the Figure 5.6 state with the Figure 5.7 keys and FKs.

    (a) Insert Robert Scott into EMPLOYEE

    Ssn 943775543 is new (no key violation) and not NULL; Super_ssn 888665555 exists (James Borg); Dno 1 exists (Headquarters). No constraint violated: accepted.

    (b) Insert ⟨\langle⟨ProductA, 4, Bellaire, 2⟩\rangle⟩ into PROJECT

    Pnumber 4 and Pname ProductA are new. Referential integrity violated: Dnum = 2, but there is no DEPARTMENT with Dnumber 2 (only 1, 4, 5). Enforcement: reject the insertion; or correct it by changing Dnum to an existing department (1, 4 or 5) or NULL (if Dnum may be NULL); or first insert a DEPARTMENT tuple with Dnumber 2 (which must itself satisfy its constraints, e.g. a valid Mgr_ssn), then accept.

    (c) Insert ⟨\langle⟨Production, 4, 943775543, 2007-10-01⟩\rangle⟩ into DEPARTMENT

    Key constraint violated: Dnumber 4 already exists (Administration). Referential integrity violated: Mgr_ssn 943775543 does not exist in EMPLOYEE. Enforcement: reject; or correct by giving an unused Dnumber (e.g. 6) and either a Mgr_ssn of an existing employee or first inserting employee 943775543 (operation (a)) before this insert.

    (d) Insert ⟨\langle⟨677678989, NULL, 40.0⟩\rangle⟩ into WORKS_ON

    Entity integrity violated: Pno is part of the primary key {Essn, Pno} and is NULL. Referential integrity violated: Essn 677678989 does not exist in EMPLOYEE. (Pno NULL is not an RI violation by itself, since an FK may be NULL; it is ruled out by entity integrity.) Enforcement: reject; or ask for a valid Pno (an existing Pnumber) and a valid Essn (or insert the employee 677678989 first).

    (e) Insert ⟨\langle⟨453453453, John, M, 1990-12-12, spouse⟩\rangle⟩ into DEPENDENT

    Essn 453453453 exists (Joyce English); key (453453453, John) is new and not NULL. No constraint violated: accepted. (If Relationship had an enumerated domain {Spouse, Son, Daughter}, the lowercase ‘spouse’ could be a domain violation; the schema declares no such domain, so it is accepted.)

    (f) Delete WORKS_ON tuples with Essn = 333445555

    Deletes 4 tuples (Pno 2, 3, 10, 20). Nothing references WORKS_ON, and Delete can only violate RI. No violation: accepted.

    (g) Delete EMPLOYEE 987654321 (Jennifer Wallace)

    Referential integrity violated in four relations, because this tuple is referenced by:

    • EMPLOYEE.Super_ssn of 999887777 (Alicia Zelaya) and 987987987 (Ahmad Jabbar);
    • DEPARTMENT.Mgr_ssn of department 4 (Administration);
    • WORKS_ON tuples (987654321, 30) and (987654321, 20);
    • DEPENDENT tuple (987654321, Abner).

    Enforcement options: restrict (reject the delete); cascade: delete the WORKS_ON and DEPENDENT tuples (sensible: they depend on the employee); set null for Super_ssn of the two supervisees (allowed: not part of a PK) and for Mgr_ssn (only if the department may be without a manager); set default/another valid value, e.g. make 888665555 the new supervisor and manager of department 4. Set null is not possible for WORKS_ON.Essn or DEPENDENT.Essn (part of the PK). Cascading into EMPLOYEE or DEPARTMENT (deleting Alicia, Ahmad or the department) would not make sense.

    (h) Delete the PROJECT tuple with Pname = ProductX (Pnumber 1)

    Referential integrity violated: WORKS_ON tuples (123456789, 1) and (453453453, 1) reference project 1. Enforcement: reject; or cascade (delete those two WORKS_ON tuples, the natural choice for a relationship relation); set null is impossible (Pno is part of WORKS_ON’s PK); or set them to a default/other project.

    (i) Department 5: Mgr_ssn := 123456789, Mgr_start_date := 2007-10-01

    123456789 exists (John Smith) and works in department 5; the date is a valid date. No violation: accepted. (If Mgr_ssn were declared UNIQUE, it would still be fine: Smith manages no other department.)

    (j) Super_ssn of 999887777 := 943775543

    Referential integrity violated: no EMPLOYEE has Ssn 943775543 in the Figure 5.6 state. Enforcement: reject; or use an existing supervisor Ssn or NULL; or first insert employee 943775543 (as in (a)).

    (k) Hours of WORKS_ON (999887777, 10) := 5.0

    Hours is neither a key nor an FK; 5.0 is in its domain. No violation: accepted.

    Answer
    a, e, f, i, kno violation (accepted)
    bRI (Dnum 2 does not exist)
    ckey (Dnumber 4 exists) + RI (Mgr_ssn 943775543 does not exist)
    dentity integrity (Pno NULL in PK) + RI (Essn 677678989 does not exist)
    gRI: referenced by EMPLOYEE (2 supervisees), DEPARTMENT 4, WORKS_ON (2), DEPENDENT (1)
    hRI: referenced by WORKS_ON (2 tuples)
    jRI (Super_ssn 943775543 does not exist)
    What the grader checks

    For each operation the marker wants: the named constraint(s), the specific offending value/tuple (“Dnum = 2 has no DEPARTMENT”), and for violations the enforcement options (reject / cascade / set null / set default) with which ones are legal. Typical deductions: missing the second violation in (c) or (d); saying a delete violates entity integrity; proposing set null on a PK attribute; treating (a) or (j) as if the earlier insert had happened.

    5.12AIRLINE reservation update and its constraintsE&N Ex. 5.12 · p. 171

    Consider the AIRLINE relational database schema shown in Figure 5.8, which describes a database for airline flight information. Each FLIGHT is identified by a Flight_number, and consists of one or more FLIGHT_LEGs with Leg_numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on. Each FLIGHT_LEG has scheduled arrival and departure times, airports, and one or more LEG_INSTANCEs—one for each Date on which the flight travels. FAREs are kept for each FLIGHT. For each FLIGHT_LEG instance, SEAT_RESERVATIONs are kept, as are the AIRPLANE used on the leg and the actual arrival and departure times and airports. An AIRPLANE is identified by an Airplane_id and is of a particular AIRPLANE_TYPE. CAN_LAND relates AIRPLANE_TYPEs to the AIRPORTs at which they can land. An AIRPORT is identified by an Airport_code. Consider an update for the AIRLINE database to enter a reservation on a particular flight or flight leg on a given date.

    1. Give the operations for this update.
    2. What types of constraints would you expect to check?
    3. Which of these constraints are key, entity integrity, and referential integrity constraints, and which are not?
    4. Specify all the referential integrity constraints that hold on the schema shown in Figure 5.8.

    Figure 5.8 (PKs underlined): AIRPORT(Airport_code, Name, City, State); FLIGHT(Flight_number, Airline, Weekdays); FLIGHT_LEG(Flight_number, Leg_number, Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time); LEG_INSTANCE(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Number_of_available_seats, Airplane_id, Departure_airport_code, Departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Arrival_time); FARE(Flight_number, Fare_code, Amount, Restrictions); AIRPLANE_TYPE(Airplane_type_name, Max_seats, Company); CAN_LAND(Airplane_type_name, Airport_code); AIRPLANE(Airplane_id, Total_number_of_seats, Airplane_type); SEAT_RESERVATION(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number, Customer_name, Customer_phone).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. A reservation on a flight on a date means one seat on each of its legs on that date; a reservation on a leg is the one-leg case. Why: seats are recorded per LEG_INSTANCE.
    2. Number_of_available_seats is maintained by the application (it is stored, so it must be updated).

    (a) Operations

    For each leg LLL of the flight being booked (just one if a single leg is booked), on date DDD:

    1. (Read) check LEG_INSTANCE(FFF, LLL, DDD) exists and Number_of_available_seats >0> 0>0; choose a free Seat_number (no SEAT_RESERVATION(FFF,LLL,DDD, seat) yet).
    2. Insert ⟨F,L,D,Seat_number,Customer_name,Customer_phone⟩\langle F, L, D, \textit{Seat\_number}, \textit{Customer\_name}, \textit{Customer\_phone}\rangle⟨F,L,D,Seat_number,Customer_name,Customer_phone⟩ into SEAT_RESERVATION.
    3. Update LEG_INSTANCE(FFF,LLL,DDD): Number_of_available_seats := Number_of_available_seats −-− 1.

    All of these form one transaction, so a multi-leg booking either succeeds on every leg or not at all.

    (b) Constraints to check

    • the seat is not already taken for that leg instance (uniqueness of the SEAT_RESERVATION key);
    • no NULL in Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number;
    • the leg instance being reserved exists;
    • domains: valid date, seat number format, phone format, available seats is a non-negative integer;
    • Number_of_available_seats >0> 0>0 before booking and ≥0\geq 0≥0 after;
    • Seat_number must be a real seat of the AIRPLANE assigned to that leg instance (at most Total_number_of_seats);
    • Number_of_available_seats = Total_number_of_seats of the assigned airplane −-− number of reservations for that leg instance;
    • for a whole-flight booking, the date is one on which the flight operates (Weekdays) and every leg gets a reservation.

    (c) Classification

    TypeConstraint from (b)
    Key constraintSeat not already reserved: PK {Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number} of SEAT_RESERVATION unique
    Entity integrityNone of Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number is NULL
    Referential integrity(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date) of the new reservation must exist in LEG_INSTANCE
    Domain constraintsValid date, phone, seat-number format; available seats a non-negative integer
    Not key/EI/RI (semantic, application-enforced)available seats >0>0>0 before / ≥0\ge 0≥0 after; seat number within the assigned airplane’s seats; available seats consistent with the count of reservations; flight operates on that weekday; all legs booked together

    (d) All referential integrity constraints on Figure 5.8

    Referencing relationForeign keyReferences
    FLIGHT_LEGFlight_numberFLIGHT.Flight_number
    FLIGHT_LEGDeparture_airport_codeAIRPORT.Airport_code
    FLIGHT_LEGArrival_airport_codeAIRPORT.Airport_code
    LEG_INSTANCE(Flight_number, Leg_number)FLIGHT_LEG.(Flight_number, Leg_number)
    LEG_INSTANCEAirplane_idAIRPLANE.Airplane_id
    LEG_INSTANCEDeparture_airport_codeAIRPORT.Airport_code
    LEG_INSTANCEArrival_airport_codeAIRPORT.Airport_code
    FAREFlight_numberFLIGHT.Flight_number
    CAN_LANDAirplane_type_nameAIRPLANE_TYPE. Airplane_type_name
    CAN_LANDAirport_codeAIRPORT.Airport_code
    AIRPLANEAirplane_typeAIRPLANE_TYPE. Airplane_type_name
    SEAT_RESERVATION(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date)LEG_INSTANCE.(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date)

    Twelve RI constraints. The composite FKs reference the whole composite key: LEG_INSTANCE references FLIGHT_LEG (not FLIGHT), and SEAT_RESERVATION references LEG_INSTANCE (not FLIGHT_LEG).     5.15Foreign keys: sales tripsE&N Ex. 5.15 · p. 173

    Consider the following relations for a database that keeps track of business trips of salespersons in a sales office: SALESPERSON(Ssn, Name, Start_year, Dept_no); TRIP(Ssn, From_city, To_city, Departure_date, Return_date, Trip_id); EXPENSE(Trip_id, Account#, Amount). A trip can be charged to one or more accounts. Specify the foreign keys for this schema, stating any assumptions you make.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Each trip is made by exactly one salesperson (Ssn is a single-valued attribute of TRIP, not part of its key).
    2. There is no ACCOUNT or DEPARTMENT relation in the schema, so Account# and Dept_no are not FKs here. Why: a FK must reference the PK of an existing relation. If such relations were added, Account# → ACCOUNT and Dept_no → DEPARTMENT would be FKs too.
    Answer

    TRIP.Ssn → SALESPERSON.Ssn (NOT NULL: every trip has a salesperson);  EXPENSE.Trip_id → TRIP.Trip_id.

    Because a trip can be charged to several accounts, Trip_id alone does not identify an EXPENSE tuple; the PK is {Trip_id, Account#} and only its Trip_id part is a FK. Suitable actions: ON DELETE CASCADE for EXPENSE.Trip_id (expenses belong to the trip), RESTRICT for TRIP.Ssn (keep trip history).

    5.16Foreign keys: enrolment and book adoptionE&N Ex. 5.16 · p. 173

    Consider the following relations for a database that keeps track of student enrollment in courses and the books adopted for each course: STUDENT(Ssn, Name, Major, Bdate); COURSE(Course#, Cname, Dept); ENROLL(Ssn, Course#, Quarter, Grade); BOOK_ADOPTION(Course#, Quarter, Book_isbn); TEXT(Book_isbn, Book_title, Publisher, Author). Specify the foreign keys for this schema, stating any assumptions you make.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Major and Dept are plain attributes (there is no DEPARTMENT relation to reference).
    2. A course may adopt a book in a quarter even if nobody has enrolled yet, so BOOK_ADOPTION does not reference ENROLL. Why: (Course#, Quarter) is not a key of ENROLL anyway, so it could not be a FK to it.
    Answer

    ENROLL.Ssn → STUDENT.Ssn;  ENROLL.Course# → COURSE.Course#;  BOOK_ADOPTION.Course# → COURSE.Course#;  BOOK_ADOPTION.Book_isbn → TEXT.Book_isbn.

    Book_isbn is not part of BOOK_ADOPTION’s key, so as given only one book is adopted per course per quarter; Book_isbn should be NOT NULL (an adoption without a book is meaningless).

    5.17Car dealership: FKs and RI-violating insertsE&N Ex. 5.17 · p. 173★ Must-do

    Consider the following relations for a database that keeps track of automobile sales in a car dealership (OPTION refers to some optional equipment installed on an automobile): CAR(Serial_no, Model, Manufacturer, Price); OPTION(Serial_no, Option_name, Price); SALE(Salesperson_id, Serial_no, Date, Sale_price); SALESPERSON(Salesperson_id, Name, Phone). First, specify the foreign keys for this schema, stating any assumptions you make. Next, populate the relations with a few sample tuples, and then give an example of an insertion in the SALE and SALESPERSON relations that violates the referential integrity constraints and of another insertion that does not.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. OPTION records options installed on a specific car (identified by its Serial_no). Why: its PK contains Serial_no.
    2. A car can be sold jointly by several salespersons (that is why SALE’s PK is {Salesperson_id, Serial_no}); Sale_price is the price of the whole sale.

    Foreign keys

    OPTION.Serial_no → CAR.Serial_no;  SALE.Serial_no → CAR.Serial_no;  SALE.Salesperson_id → SALESPERSON.Salesperson_id. CAR and SALESPERSON have no FKs.

    Sample (valid) state

    CAR
    Serial_noModelManufacturerPrice
    C1CivicHonda20000
    C2CorollaToyota22000
    C3NexonTata15000

     

    OPTION
    Serial_noOption_namePrice
    C1Sunroof800
    C1GPS300
    C2GPS300
    SALESPERSON
    Salesperson_idNamePhone
    S1Asha98480-11111
    S2Ravi98480-22222

     

    SALE
    Salesperson_idSerial_noDateSale_price
    S1C12026-01-1021500
    S2C22026-02-0322000

    Insertions

    InsertionResult
    SALE ⟨\langle⟨S3, C3, 2026-03-01, 15000⟩\rangle⟩Violates RI: no SALESPERSON S3.
    SALE ⟨\langle⟨S1, C9, 2026-03-01, 18000⟩\rangle⟩Violates RI: no CAR C9.
    SALE ⟨\langle⟨S2, C3, 2026-03-01, 14500⟩\rangle⟩Valid: S2 and C3 both exist; key (S2, C3) is new.
    SALESPERSON ⟨\langle⟨S3, Meera, 98480-33333⟩\rangle⟩Valid: new key, no FKs to check.
    SALESPERSON ⟨\langle⟨S1, Kiran, 98480-44444⟩\rangle⟩Rejected, but by the key constraint (S1 exists), not RI.

    SALESPERSON has no foreign key, so no insertion into SALESPERSON can violate referential integrity; RI can be violated by inserting into a referencing relation (SALE, OPTION) only. A SALESPERSON can only cause RI trouble by being deleted or having its Salesperson_id updated while referenced by SALE. (All five insertions were checked in SQLite with foreign keys enforced.)

    What the grader checks

    Expected: all three FKs (with direction), a populated valid state, one violating and one non-violating insert for SALE, and the observation about SALESPERSON. Common deductions: inventing an RI violation for an insert into SALESPERSON; listing CAR.Serial_no as a FK; populating a state that is itself invalid.

    5.20Natural versus surrogate keysE&N Ex. 5.20 · p. 174

    Recent changes in privacy laws have disallowed organizations from using Social Security numbers to identify individuals unless certain restrictions are satisfied. As a result, most U.S. universities cannot use SSNs as primary keys (except for financial data). In practice, Student_id, a unique identifier assigned to every student, is likely to be used as the primary key rather than SSN since Student_id can be used throughout the system.

    1. Some database designers are reluctant to use generated keys (also known as surrogate keys) for primary keys (such as Student_id) because they are artificial. Can you propose any natural choices of keys that can be used to identify the student record in a UNIVERSITY database?
    2. Suppose that you are able to guarantee uniqueness of a natural key that includes last name. Are you guaranteed that the last name will not change during the lifetime of the database? If last name can change, what solutions can you propose for creating a primary key that still includes last name but remains unique?
    3. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using generated (surrogate) keys?
    Solution · written for this guide

    (a) Natural candidate keys

    • A national/official identifier other than SSN: passport number (+ issuing country), Aadhaar-style ID, driver’s licence number + issuing state. Not every student has one, and the same privacy concerns may apply.
    • University e-mail address / login name (unique by construction, but assigned by the university, so half-artificial, and can be renamed).
    • A combination such as {Last_name, First_name, Birth_date, Birth_place} or {Name, Birth_date, Home_phone}: usually unique, but uniqueness is not guaranteed and values may be missing (NULLs are forbidden in a PK) or change.

    (b) Last name can change

    No: last names change (marriage, divorce, legal name change, corrections of spelling). A PK must be stable, because it is copied into every referencing FK. Solutions that keep the last name in the key:

    • use the name at admission (Admission_last_name), never updated, and store the current name in a separate non-key attribute (optionally with a NAME_HISTORY relation);
    • append a disambiguating sequence number or the admission year: {Admission_last_name, Seq_no} or {Last_name, Birth_date, Seq_no};
    • if the key must follow the current name, declare all FKs ON UPDATE CASCADE so a name change is propagated (costly, and still needs a tie-breaker for uniqueness).

    (c) Surrogate keys

    AdvantagesDisadvantages
    Guaranteed unique and never NULL (system generated)No real-world meaning: users cannot recall or verify it; needs a lookup
    Stable: never needs to change, so no cascading FK updatesDoes not stop duplicates of the same real person (two Student_ids for one student) unless the natural key is also declared UNIQUE
    Short, single attribute: compact FKs, fast joins and indexesAn extra attribute and index; queries need joins to show meaningful values
    Avoids exposing sensitive data (SSN)Generation must be coordinated (sequences) when merging databases

    Good practice: surrogate PK plus a UNIQUE constraint on the best natural key.
