    9.2Map the UNIVERSITY ER schemaE&N Ex. 9.2 · p. 303★ Must-do

    Map the UNIVERSITY database schema shown in Figure 3.20 into a relational database schema.

    Figure 3.20 (summary). Entity types and attributes (keys underlined): COLLEGE(CName, COffice, CPhone); INSTRUCTOR(Id, IName, Rank, IOffice, IPhone); DEPT(DName, DCode, DOffice, DPhone); STUDENT(SId, SName(FName, MName, LName), DOB, Addr, Phone, Major); COURSE(CCode, CoName, Credits, Level, CDesc); SECTION(SecId, SecNo, Sem, Year, DaysTime, CRoom(Bldg, RoomNo)). Relationship types with (min,max) of each participant: DEAN: COLLEGE (1,1), INSTRUCTOR (0,1); ADMINS: COLLEGE (0,N), DEPT (1,1); CHAIR [attribute CStartDate]: DEPT (1,1), INSTRUCTOR (0,1); EMPLOYS: DEPT (0,N), INSTRUCTOR (1,1); HAS: DEPT (0,N), STUDENT (0,1); OFFERS: DEPT (0,N), COURSE (1,1); SECS: COURSE (0,N), SECTION (1,1); TEACHES: INSTRUCTOR (0,N), SECTION (1,1); TAKES [attribute Grade]: STUDENT (0,N), SECTION (5,N).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. (min,max) is read in the book’s notation: the pair next to an entity type says in how many relationship instances each of its entities takes part. So DEPT (1,1) in ADMINS means every department is administered by exactly one college: ADMINS is 1:N with DEPT on the N-side. Max 1 on both sides means 1:1.
    2. PKs: DCode for DEPT (short code; DName becomes UNIQUE), CCode for COURSE (CoName UNIQUE), SecId for SECTION. Why: single-attribute, stable codes are the better primary keys.
    3. HAS (student’s department) and the attribute Major are both kept, as the diagram has both; HAS is optional (0,1), so its FK is nullable.

    Step 1: regular entity types

    COLLEGE(CName, COffice, CPhone); INSTRUCTOR(Id, IName, Rank, IOffice, IPhone); DEPT(DCode, DName, DOffice, DPhone) with DName UNIQUE; STUDENT(SId, FName, MName, LName, DOB, Addr, Phone, Major) (composite SName split); COURSE(CCode, CoName, Credits, Level, CDesc) with CoName UNIQUE; SECTION(SecId, SecNo, Sem, Year, DaysTime, Bldg, RoomNo) (composite CRoom split).

    Step 2: weak entity types

    None (SECTION has its own key SecId).

    Step 3: 1:1 relationships (FK approach, total side holds the FK)

    DEAN: COLLEGE is total (1,1), so COLLEGE gets Dean_id → INSTRUCTOR.Id, NOT NULL, UNIQUE.
    CHAIR: DEPT is total (1,1), so DEPT gets Chair_id → INSTRUCTOR.Id, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, plus the relationship attribute CStartDate.

    Step 4: 1:N relationships (FK on the N-side)

    ADMINS: DEPT.CName → COLLEGE.CName, NOT NULL (DEPT (1,1)).
    EMPLOYS: INSTRUCTOR.DCode → DEPT.DCode, NOT NULL.
    HAS: STUDENT.DCode → DEPT.DCode, nullable (STUDENT (0,1)).
    OFFERS: COURSE.DCode → DEPT.DCode, NOT NULL.
    SECS: SECTION.CCode → COURSE.CCode, NOT NULL.
    TEACHES: SECTION.Instr_id → INSTRUCTOR.Id, NOT NULL.

    Step 5: M:N relationships

    TAKES: TAKES(SId, SecId, Grade), SId → STUDENT.SId, SecId → SECTION.SecId. Grade is the relationship’s attribute, so it lives here.

    Steps 6–7

    No multivalued attributes and no n-ary relationships.

    Answer

    COLLEGE(CName, COffice, CPhone, Dean_id)
    INSTRUCTOR(Id, IName, Rank, IOffice, IPhone, DCode)
    DEPT(DCode, DName, DOffice, DPhone, CName, Chair_id, CStartDate)
    STUDENT(SId, FName, MName, LName, DOB, Addr, Phone, Major, DCode)
    COURSE(CCode, CoName, Credits, Level, CDesc, DCode)
    SECTION(SecId, SecNo, Sem, Year, DaysTime, Bldg, RoomNo, CCode, Instr_id)
    TAKES(SId, SecId, Grade)
    FKs: COLLEGE.Dean_id → INSTRUCTOR.Id (NOT NULL, UNIQUE); INSTRUCTOR.DCode → DEPT.DCode (NOT NULL); DEPT.CName → COLLEGE.CName (NOT NULL); DEPT.Chair_id → INSTRUCTOR.Id (NOT NULL, UNIQUE); STUDENT.DCode → DEPT.DCode; COURSE.DCode → DEPT.DCode (NOT NULL); SECTION.CCode → COURSE.CCode (NOT NULL); SECTION.Instr_id → INSTRUCTOR.Id (NOT NULL); TAKES.SId → STUDENT.SId; TAKES.SecId → SECTION.SecId. Unique keys: DEPT.DName, COURSE.CoName, and (from Exercise 3.16) SECTION (CCode, SecNo, Sem, Year).

    Not enforceable by the schema: TAKES requires at least 5 students per section (SECTION (5,N)); this needs an assertion or application check. Note the cycle DEPT → INSTRUCTOR → DEPT (chair / employs): with both FKs NOT NULL, the first department and its chair must be inserted in one transaction with deferred constraint checking.

    What the grader checks

    Checked against the EtoR rubric: every entity mapped with a PK (M1); each 1:N FK on the N-side (M4: e.g. DCode in INSTRUCTOR, not an instructor list in DEPT); TAKES as a separate relation with both keys in its PK (M5); Grade in TAKES (M7); composites split (m3); NOT NULL for (1,1) participations (m6); UNIQUE on Dean_id and Chair_id (m7); FK arrows (M9/M10); assumptions stated (m7/m9).

    9.3Reverse-engineer the LIBRARY schema into an ER schemaE&N Ex. 9.3 · p. 303★ Must-do

    Try to map the relational schema in Figure 6.14 into an ER schema. This is part of a process known as reverse engineering, where a conceptual schema is created for an existing implemented database. State any assumptions you make.

    The schema (the LIBRARY database, Figure 6.6 in the 7th edition; PKs underlined, arrows as FKs): BOOK(Book_id, Title, Publisher_name); BOOK_AUTHORS(Book_id, Author_name); PUBLISHER(Name, Address, Phone); BOOK_COPIES(Book_id, Branch_id, No_of_copies); BOOK_LOANS(Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no, Date_out, Due_date); LIBRARY_BRANCH(Branch_id, Branch_name, Address); BORROWER(Card_no, Name, Address, Phone). FKs: BOOK.Publisher_name → PUBLISHER.Name; BOOK_AUTHORS.Book_id → BOOK; BOOK_COPIES.Book_id → BOOK; BOOK_COPIES.Branch_id → LIBRARY_BRANCH; BOOK_LOANS.Book_id → BOOK; BOOK_LOANS.Branch_id → LIBRARY_BRANCH; BOOK_LOANS.Card_no → BORROWER.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The book’s “Figure 6.14” is a cross-reference from an older edition; in the 7th edition the relational schema with FK arrows is the LIBRARY schema, Figure 6.6 (also asked as 2024 Quiz 2 Q3).
    2. Publisher_name is NOT NULL (every book has a publisher). Why: a book record without a publisher is unusual; if it may be NULL, BOOK’s participation in PUBLISHED_BY is partial instead.
    3. BOOK_LOANS records one loan of a copy of a book from a branch to a borrower; its key {Book_id, Branch_id, Card_no} means a borrower has at most one current loan of a given book from a given branch.

    Reverse mapping, relation by relation (the mapping steps run backwards)

    RelationRecognised asReason
    BOOK, PUBLISHER, LIBRARY_BRANCH, BORROWERRegular entity types (Step 1)Own single-attribute PK, not composed of FKs
    BOOK. Publisher_name1:N relationship PUBLISHED_BY (Step 4)Non-key FK in BOOK: each book has one publisher, a publisher many books; BOOK on the N-side, total
    BOOK_AUTHORSMultivalued attribute Authors of BOOK (Step 6)PK = {owner key, one value}, no other attributes
    BOOK_COPIESM:N relationship BOOK_COPIES between BOOK and LIBRARY_BRANCH, attribute No_of_copies (Step 5)PK = the two FKs; an extra non-key attribute describing the pair
    BOOK_LOANSTernary relationship BOOK_LOANS among BOOK, LIBRARY_BRANCH, BORROWER, attributes Date_out, Due_date (Step 7)PK = three FKs, so each participant is on the “many” side
    Answer

    Entity types BOOK (key Book_id, multivalued Authors), PUBLISHER (key Name), LIBRARY_BRANCH (key Branch_id), BORROWER (key Card_no); 1:N PUBLISHED_BY (PUBLISHER 1 : N BOOK, BOOK total); M:N BOOK_COPIES (BOOK–LIBRARY_BRANCH, attribute No_of_copies); ternary BOOK_LOANS (BOOK, LIBRARY_BRANCH, BORROWER; attributes Date_out, Due_date).

    Alternatives (valid if stated): BOOK_LOANS as a weak entity type LOAN identified by BOOK, BRANCH and BORROWER; a loan as a binary relationship between BORROWER and an entity COPY (if copies were individually identified); BOOK_AUTHORS as a weak entity AUTHOR with partial key Author_name (only sensible if authors had more attributes). A ternary is preferred here because the three-part key records which branch lent the book.

    What the grader checks

    Marks for: identifying each relation’s role (entity / relationship / multivalued attribute) from its key and FKs, the correct cardinalities (non-key FK = 1:N with the FK on the N-side), relationship attributes on the relationship, and a stated assumption on the ternary.

    9.4Map the SHIP_TRACKING ER schemaE&N Ex. 9.4 · p. 304

    Figure 9.8 shows an ER schema for a database that can be used to keep track of transport ships and their locations for maritime authorities. Map this schema into a relational schema and specify all primary keys and foreign keys.

    Figure 9.8 (summary). Regular entity types: SHIP(Sname, Owner); SHIP_TYPE(Type, Tonnage, Hull); STATE/COUNTRY(Name, Continent); SEA/OCEAN/LAKE(Name). Weak entity types: SHIP_MOVEMENT (partial key Time_stamp, a composite of Date and Time; attributes Longitude, Latitude), owner SHIP through identifying relationship HISTORY (SHIP 1 : N SHIP_MOVEMENT, total); PORT (partial key Pname), owner STATE/COUNTRY through identifying relationship IN (STATE/COUNTRY 1 : N PORT, total); PORT_VISIT (partial key Start_date, attribute End_date) identified through the identifying relationship SHIP_AT_PORT with SHIP (0,*) and PORT (0,*), PORT_VISIT (1,1). Other relationships: TYPE (SHIP N, total : 1 SHIP_TYPE); HOME_PORT (SHIP N : 1 PORT); ON (PORT N, total : 1 SEA/OCEAN/LAKE).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. PORT_VISIT is a weak entity with two owners (SHIP and PORT) via the ternary-like identifying relationship SHIP_AT_PORT; by Step 2 its PK is both owners’ keys plus Start_date. Why: that is the algorithm’s rule; a ship cannot be in two ports at once, so {Sname, Start_date} would also be unique, and could be chosen with this stated assumption.
    2. Relations are named STATE_COUNTRY and SEA_OCEAN_LAKE (“/” is not allowed in a name).

    Step 1: regular entities

    SHIP(Sname, Owner); SHIP_TYPE(Type, Tonnage, Hull); STATE_COUNTRY(Name, Continent); SEA_OCEAN_LAKE(Name).

    Step 2: weak entities (owners mapped first)

    PORT(SC_name, Pname): owner STATE_COUNTRY, so PK = owner key + partial key; SC_name → STATE_COUNTRY.Name.
    SHIP_MOVEMENT(Sname, Date, Time, Longitude, Latitude): owner SHIP; the composite partial key Time_stamp is split into Date and Time; Sname → SHIP.Sname.
    PORT_VISIT(Sname, SC_name, Pname, Start_date, End_date): owners SHIP and PORT (PORT’s key is itself composite, so the whole {SC_name, Pname} is carried); Sname → SHIP.Sname, (SC_name, Pname) → PORT.(SC_name, Pname). Identifying relationships HISTORY, IN, SHIP_AT_PORT need no relation.

    Step 4: 1:N relationships

    TYPE: SHIP.Type → SHIP_TYPE.Type, NOT NULL (SHIP total).
    HOME_PORT: SHIP.(Home_SC_name, Home_Pname) → PORT.(SC_name, Pname) (composite FK, nullable).
    ON: PORT.SOL_name → SEA_OCEAN_LAKE.Name, NOT NULL (PORT total).

    Steps 3, 5, 6, 7

    No 1:1, M:N, multivalued or n-ary (non-identifying) relationships.

    Answer

    SHIP(Sname, Owner, Type, Home_SC_name, Home_Pname)
    SHIP_TYPE(Type, Tonnage, Hull)
    SHIP_MOVEMENT(Sname, Date, Time, Longitude, Latitude)
    PORT_VISIT(Sname, SC_name, Pname, Start_date, End_date)
    PORT(SC_name, Pname, SOL_name)
    STATE_COUNTRY(Name, Continent)   SEA_OCEAN_LAKE(Name)
    FKs: SHIP.Type → SHIP_TYPE.Type (NOT NULL); SHIP.(Home_SC_name, Home_Pname) → PORT; SHIP_MOVEMENT.Sname → SHIP.Sname; PORT_VISIT.Sname → SHIP.Sname; PORT_VISIT.(SC_name, Pname) → PORT; PORT.SC_name → STATE_COUNTRY.Name; PORT.SOL_name → SEA_OCEAN_LAKE.Name (NOT NULL).

    What the grader checks

    Typical deductions here: PORT keyed by Pname alone (M2, its owner’s key is missing), which then makes every FK to PORT reference only part of its key (M3, counted once if consistent); Time_stamp kept as one attribute (m3); HISTORY or IN made into extra relations (m5); missing NOT NULL on SHIP.Type and PORT.SOL_name (m6).

    9.5Map BANK, AIRLINE and the other Chapter 3 schemasE&N Ex. 9.5 · p. 304

    Map the BANK ER schema of Exercise 3.23 (shown in Figure 3.21) into a relational schema. Specify all primary keys and foreign keys. Repeat for the AIRLINE schema (Figure 3.20) of Exercise 3.19 and for the other schemas for Exercises 3.16 through 3.24.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The figure numbers in the question are off by one (older edition): in the 7th edition the BANK schema is Figure 3.22 and the AIRLINE schema is Figure 3.21; those are mapped here.
    2. Exercise 3.16 uses the UNIVERSITY schema of Figure 3.20, mapped in Exercise 9.2. Exercises 3.20–3.22 ask the student to design their own ER diagrams; the standard designs below are mapped, with their assumptions.

    (1) BANK (Figure 3.22)

    Diagram: BANK(Code, Name, Addr); weak BANK_BRANCH(partial key Branch_no, Addr) owned by BANK via identifying BRANCHES (1:N, total); ACCOUNT(Acct_no, Balance, Type) and LOAN(Loan_no, Amount, Type); ACCTS: BANK_BRANCH 1 : N ACCOUNT (ACCOUNT total); LOANS: BANK_BRANCH 1 : N LOAN (LOAN total); CUSTOMER(Ssn, Name, Phone, Addr); A_C: ACCOUNT M : N CUSTOMER (ACCOUNT total); L_C: LOAN M : N CUSTOMER (LOAN total).

    Steps

    Step 1: BANK(Code, Name, Addr); ACCOUNT(Acct_no, Balance, Type); LOAN(Loan_no, Amount, Type); CUSTOMER(Ssn, Name, Phone, Addr). Step 2: BANK_BRANCH(Bank_code, Branch_no, Addr), Bank_code → BANK.Code. Step 4: ACCTS and LOANS put the full branch key (Bank_code, Branch_no) into ACCOUNT and LOAN as a NOT NULL composite FK. Step 5: A_C(Ssn, Acct_no) and L_C(Ssn, Loan_no).

    Answer

    BANK(Code, Name, Addr); BANK_BRANCH(Bank_code, Branch_no, Addr); ACCOUNT(Acct_no, Balance, Type, Bank_code, Branch_no); LOAN(Loan_no, Amount, Type, Bank_code, Branch_no); CUSTOMER(Ssn, Name, Phone, Addr); A_C(Ssn, Acct_no); L_C(Ssn, Loan_no).
    FKs: BANK_BRANCH.Bank_code → BANK.Code; ACCOUNT.(Bank_code, Branch_no) → BANK_BRANCH (NOT NULL); LOAN.(Bank_code, Branch_no) → BANK_BRANCH (NOT NULL); A_C.Ssn → CUSTOMER.Ssn; A_C.Acct_no → ACCOUNT.Acct_no; L_C.Ssn → CUSTOMER.Ssn; L_C.Loan_no → LOAN.Loan_no.

    Total participation of ACCOUNT in A_C and LOAN in L_C (every account/loan has a customer) cannot be enforced by an FK (it is on the M:N side); it needs an assertion.

    (2) AIRLINE (Figure 3.21)

    Diagram: AIRPORT(Airport_code, Name, City, State); FLIGHT(Number, Airline, Weekdays); weak FLIGHT_LEG(partial key Leg_no) owned by FLIGHT (LEGS); DEPARTURE_AIRPORT and ARRIVAL_AIRPORT: AIRPORT 1 : N FLIGHT_LEG (FLIGHT_LEG total) with attributes Scheduled_dep_time / Scheduled_arr_time; weak FARE (partial key Code; Amount, Restrictions) owned by FLIGHT (FARES); weak LEG_INSTANCE (partial key Date; No_of_avail_seats) owned by FLIGHT_LEG (INSTANCE_OF); DEPARTS/ARRIVES: AIRPORT 1 : N LEG_INSTANCE with Dep_time / Arr_time; ASSIGNED: AIRPLANE 1 : N LEG_INSTANCE (LEG_INSTANCE total); AIRPLANE(Airplane_id, Total_no_of_seats); TYPE: AIRPLANE_TYPE 1 : N AIRPLANE (AIRPLANE total); AIRPLANE_TYPE(Type_name, Max_seats, Company); CAN_LAND: AIRPORT M : N AIRPLANE_TYPE; weak SEAT (partial key Seat_no) owned by LEG_INSTANCE via the identifying relationship RESERVATION (attributes Customer_name, Cphone).

    Steps

    Step 1: AIRPORT, FLIGHT, AIRPLANE_TYPE, AIRPLANE. Step 2 (owners first): FLIGHT_LEG(Flight_number, Leg_number); FARE(Flight_number, Fare_code, Amount, Restrictions); LEG_INSTANCE(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Number_of_available_seats), whose owner FLIGHT_LEG is itself weak, so it carries the full two-part key; SEAT_RESERVATION(Flight_number, Leg_number, Date, Seat_number, Customer_name, Customer_phone): the weak SEAT plus the attributes of its identifying relationship RESERVATION. Step 4: DEPARTURE_/ARRIVAL_AIRPORT add Departure_airport_code, Scheduled_departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Scheduled_arrival_time to FLIGHT_LEG (codes NOT NULL); DEPARTS/ARRIVES add Departure_airport_code, Departure_time, Arrival_airport_code, Arrival_time to LEG_INSTANCE; ASSIGNED adds Airplane_id (NOT NULL) to LEG_INSTANCE; TYPE adds Airplane_type (NOT NULL) to AIRPLANE. Step 5: CAN_LAND(Airplane_type_name, Airport_code).

    Answer

    Exactly the AIRLINE schema of Figure 5.8, with the twelve FKs listed and drawn in Exercise 5.12(d), plus NOT NULL on FLIGHT_LEG’s two airport codes, LEG_INSTANCE.Airplane_id and AIRPLANE.Airplane_type (total participations).

    (3) Exercise 3.24: COMPANY fragment (Figure 3.23)

    EMPLOYEE, DEPARTMENT, PHONE with WORKS_IN (EMPLOYEE (0,2) – DEPARTMENT), CONTAINS (DEPARTMENT (1,3) – PHONE (1,1), assuming each phone belongs to one department) and HAS_PHONE (EMPLOYEE – PHONE, M:N).

    The nested multivalued composite attribute {College_name, Start, End, {Degree, Month, Year}, {Course, Semester, Year, Grade}} maps (Step 6, applied level by level) to PREV_COLLEGE(Ssn, College_name, Start_date, End_date), PREV_DEGREE(Ssn, College_name, Degree_name, Month, Year), PREV_TRANSCRIPT(Ssn, College_name, Course_name, Semester, Year, Grade); (Ssn) → STUDENT and the two inner relations’ (Ssn, College_name) → PREV_COLLEGE (the whole key). The entity-only design of 3.18 (weak entities COLLEGE_ATTENDED, DEGREE_AWARDED, TRANSCRIPT_ENTRY) maps to the same relations by Step 2. (Assumption: a student attended a college only once.)

(Assumption: names are unique, as the exercise implies.)

    Map the EER diagrams in Figures 4.9 and 4.12 into relational schemas. Justify your choice of mapping options.

    Solution · written for this guide

    (1) Figure 4.9: UNIVERSITY

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. PERSON/{FACULTY, STUDENT} is disjoint and partial (single line from PERSON to the d circle). Option 8A. Why: 8B loses persons who are neither (partial); 8C would be legal (disjoint) but both subclasses have their own attributes and many relationships (ADVISOR, BELONGS, MAJOR, …) that must reference the subclass, so separate relations are cleaner and avoid many NULLs.
    2. STUDENT/GRAD_STUDENT (predicate Class = 5): 8A with relation GRAD_STUDENT. Why: GRAD_STUDENT has its own relationships (ADVISOR, COMMITTEE, the category) and a multivalued attribute that need a relation to reference. Membership must agree with Class = 5 (a semantic constraint, checked by the application).
    3. INSTRUCTOR_RESEARCHER is a category whose superclasses (FACULTY, GRAD_STUDENT) share the key Ssn, so (Step 9) no surrogate key is needed: INSTRUCTOR_RESEARCHER(Ssn) with Ssn → PERSON.Ssn and the constraint “Ssn is in FACULTY or GRAD_STUDENT” (assertion). A surrogate key with FKs in FACULTY and GRAD_STUDENT would also be accepted.
    4. SECTION/CURRENT_SECTION (predicate-defined): 8A, a relation CURRENT_SECTION(Sec#) so that REGISTERED can reference it. (Alternative: a view selecting the current quarter, with REGISTERED referencing SECTION.)
    5. SUPPORT’s PK is {Grant_no, Ir_ssn} (one support period per grant and person); if the same person can be supported by the same grant in several periods, add Start to the key.

Step 3: CHAIRS (1:1): DEPARTMENT.Chair_ssn → FACULTY.Ssn, UNIQUE. Step 4: ADVISOR → GRAD_STUDENT.Advisor_ssn; PI → GRANT.Pi_ssn; MINOR, MAJOR → STUDENT.Minor_dept, Major_dept; TEACH → SECTION.Instructor_ssn; CS → SECTION.C#; DC → COURSE.Dname; CD → DEPARTMENT.Cname. Step 5: COMMITTEE, BELONGS, SUPPORT, REGISTERED, TRANSCRIPT. Step 6: DEGREES(Ssn, College, Degree, Year) for the multivalued composite Degrees.

    Answer

    PERSON(Ssn, Fname, Minit, Lname, Bdate, Sex, No, Street, Apt_no, City, State, Zip)
    FACULTY(Ssn, Rank, Foffice, Fphone, Salary)  STUDENT(Ssn, Class, Major_dept, Minor_dept)

    (25 foreign keys over 19 relations; the schema diagram is omitted for size, every arrow is in the list above.)

    (2) Figure 4.12: SMALL_AIRPORT

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. OWNER is a category of CORPORATION (key Name) and PERSON (key Ssn): different keys, so Step 9 with a surrogate key Owner_id in OWNER, added as a nullable, UNIQUE FK to CORPORATION and PERSON, plus the recommended type attribute Owner_type.
    2. PILOT and EMPLOYEE are two separate subclasses of PERSON; a person may be both (a pilot who is also an employee), i.e. overlapping and partial. Option 8A. Why: PILOT and EMPLOYEE take part in their own M:N relationships (FLIES, WORKS_ON, MAINTAIN) whose FKs must reference exactly the pilots/employees; 8C cannot represent overlap; 8B is impossible (partial, and PERSON is also an owner). 8D (flags Is_pilot, Is_employee in PERSON) would be accepted with a stated assumption, but then FLIES could only reference PERSON.

Step 2: SERVICE(Reg#, Date, Workcode, Hours): composite partial key split, owner key added. Step 4: OF_TYPE → AIRPLANE.Model; STORED_IN → AIRPLANE.Hangar_number. Step 5: OWNS(Owner_id, Reg#, Pdate), WORKS_ON(Model, Emp_ssn), FLIES(Model, Pilot_ssn), MAINTAIN(Emp_ssn, Reg#, Date, Workcode) (the whole three-part SERVICE key). Step 8A: EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Salary, Shift), PILOT(Ssn, Lic_num, Restr). Step 9: OWNER(Owner_id, Owner_type); Owner_id added to CORPORATION and PERSON.

    PLANE_TYPE(Model, Capacity, Weight); HANGAR(Number, Capacity, Location); AIRPLANE(Reg#, Model, Hangar_number); SERVICE(Reg#, Date, Workcode, Hours); OWNER(Owner_id, Owner_type); CORPORATION(Name, Address, Phone, Owner_id); PERSON(Ssn, Name, Address, Phone, Owner_id); EMPLOYEE(Ssn, Salary, Shift); PILOT(Ssn, Lic_num, Restr); OWNS(Owner_id, Reg#, Pdate); WORKS_ON(Model, Emp_ssn); FLIES(Model, Pilot_ssn); MAINTAIN(Emp_ssn, Reg#, Date, Workcode). FKs as drawn below.

    What the grader checks

    For EER mappings graders look at: the Step 8 option fits the constraints (M8: 8C for overlapping subclasses is a major mistake), the Step 9 surrogate key for a category with different keys, the justification sentence for each choice, and MAINTAIN referencing the whole SERVICE key (M3).

    9.7M:N without a new relation?E&N Ex. 9.7 · p. 304

    Is it possible to successfully map a binary M:N relationship type without requiring a new relation? Why or why not?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Not in the basic (flat, 1NF) relational model.

    • A FK in one participant’s relation can hold one value per tuple. In an M:N relationship an employee works on many projects and a project has many employees, so either side would need a set of FK values (e.g. EMPLOYEE.Pnos = {1, 2}), which violates atomicity (first normal form).
    • Repeating the entity tuple once per related entity (EMPLOYEE with an extra Pno column, one row per project) destroys the entity’s key (Ssn no longer unique, PK must become {Ssn, Pno}) and stores the employee’s data redundantly, causing update anomalies; employees with no project need NULL in a key attribute. That table is in effect the relationship relation merged with EMPLOYEE, a badly normalized design.
    • Hence Step 5: a separate relationship relation whose PK is the combination of both FKs (WORKS_ON(Essn, Pno, Hours)).

    It becomes possible only outside the flat model: with multivalued/array attributes in object-relational systems (an array of FKs) or with nested relations. (Conversely, 1:1 and 1:N relationships can use the relationship relation option, but do not need it.)

    Answer

    No. Each FK holds a single atomic value, but each entity in an M:N relationship relates to many entities on the other side, so the relationship must be a separate relation with PK = both FKs (unless array/multivalued attributes are allowed, which the basic relational model forbids).

    9.8Car dealer: all four specialization optionsE&N Ex. 9.8 · p. 305★ Must-do

    Consider the EER diagram in Figure 9.9 for a car dealer. Map the EER schema into a set of relations. For the VEHICLE to CAR/TRUCK/SUV generalization, consider the four options presented in Section 9.2.1 and show the relational schema design under each of those options.

    Figure 9.9: VEHICLE(Vin, Price, Model) with a disjoint (d) and total (double line) specialization into CAR(Engine_size), TRUCK(Tonnage), SUV(No_seats); SALESPERSON(Sid, Name); CUSTOMER(Ssn, Name, Address(Street, City, State)); relationship SALE (attribute Date) among VEHICLE (N), SALESPERSON (1) and CUSTOMER (1), with CUSTOMER’s participation total (double line).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. SALE is a ternary relationship. The 1 next to SALESPERSON means: for a given (vehicle, customer) pair there is one salesperson; the 1 next to CUSTOMER: for a given (vehicle, salesperson) pair there is one customer. So a vehicle is sold at most once and Vin alone identifies a sale. By Step 7, the FKs to participants with cardinality 1 are not in the PK: PK(SALE) = {Vin}.
    2. Address is composite: stored as Street, City, State (m3).
    3. Because SALE’s PK is just Vin, it could also be folded into VEHICLE as nullable columns (Sid, Customer_ssn, Sale_date); the separate relation of Step 7 is kept because it avoids NULLs for unsold vehicles.

    Steps 1 and 7 (common to every option)

    SALESPERSON(Sid, Name)   CUSTOMER(Ssn, Name, Street, City, State)
    SALE(Vin, Sid, Customer_ssn, Date) with Sid → SALESPERSON.Sid (NOT NULL), Customer_ssn → CUSTOMER.Ssn (NOT NULL), Vin → the vehicle relation(s) (see each option). CUSTOMER’s total participation (every customer bought something) cannot be enforced by an FK (the FK is in SALE).

    Step 8, Option 8A: superclass + subclass relations

    VEHICLE(Vin, Model, Price); CAR(Vin, Engine_size); TRUCK(Vin, Tonnage); SUV(Vin, No_seats); CAR.Vin, TRUCK.Vin, SUV.Vin → VEHICLE.Vin; SALE.Vin → VEHICLE.Vin. Represents everything except that “total” and “disjoint” need an extra check (every VEHICLE Vin appears in exactly one subclass table).

    Option 8B: subclass relations only

    CAR(Vin, Model, Price, Engine_size); TRUCK(Vin, Model, Price, Tonnage); SUV(Vin, Model, Price, No_seats). Valid here because the specialization is total (no vehicle is lost) and disjoint (no vehicle is duplicated). Costs: a Vin must be unique across the three tables (not enforced by the three PKs alone); listing all vehicles needs an OUTER UNION; and SALE.Vin can no longer be a single FK (it references one of three relations), so this RI must be enforced by triggers/application.

    Option 8C: single relation with one type attribute

    VEHICLE(Vin, Model, Price, Vehicle_type, Engine_size, Tonnage, No_seats), Vehicle_type ∈\in∈ {‘Car’, ‘Truck’, ‘SUV’}, NOT NULL (total). Valid because the subclasses are disjoint. Each tuple has NULL in the two attributes that do not apply (acceptable: only one local attribute per subclass). SALE.Vin → VEHICLE.Vin.

    Option 8D: single relation with Boolean flags

    VEHICLE(Vin, Model, Price, Car_flag, Engine_size, Truck_flag, Tonnage, Suv_flag, No_seats). Designed for overlapping specializations; for this disjoint, total one we must add the check “exactly one of the three flags is true”. SALE.Vin → VEHICLE.Vin.

    Answer
    CommonSALESPERSON(Sid, Name); CUSTOMER(Ssn, Name, Street, City, State); SALE(Vin, Sid, Customer_ssn, Date)
    8AVEHICLE(Vin, Model, Price); CAR(Vin, Engine_size); TRUCK(Vin, Tonnage); SUV(Vin, No_seats)
    8BCAR(Vin, Model, Price, Engine_size); TRUCK(Vin, Model, Price, Tonnage); SUV(Vin, Model, Price, No_seats)
    8CVEHICLE(Vin, Model, Price, Vehicle_type, Engine_size, Tonnage, No_seats)
    8DVEHICLE(Vin, Model, Price, Car_flag, Truck_flag, Suv_flag, Engine_size, Tonnage, No_seats)

    All four are legal for this disjoint, total specialization. Best choices: 8C (few subclass attributes, no joins, single FK target for SALE) or 8A; 8B is the weakest (SALE.Vin has no single referenced relation).

    What the grader checks

    Marks are given per option: correct attribute placement and PK in each, plus a remark on which constraints each option captures (disjoint/total) and its drawback. Also checked: SALE mapped as a ternary relationship with the right PK (M6 in GA3), Date in SALE (M7), Address split (m3), FKs drawn (M9/M10).

    10  Exam cheat sheet

    Relational model: concepts

    • Domain: set of atomic values; name + data type + format (+ units).
    • Schema R(A1,…,An)R(A_1,\dots,A_n)R(A1​,…,An​): name + attributes; degree =n=n=n. State r(R)r(R)r(R): a set of tuples, r⊆dom(A1)×⋯×dom(An)r\subseteq \mathrm{dom}(A_1)\times\dots\times\mathrm{dom}(A_n)r⊆dom(A1​)×⋯×dom(An​); number of tuples = cardinality.
    • Schema vs state: intension (rarely changes) vs extension (changes on every update). DB schema S={Ri}S=\{R_i\}S={Ri​} + IC; a state satisfying all IC is valid.
    • Characteristics: tuples unordered (a set); values in a tuple ordered (or a mapping, alternative definition); values atomic (flat model, 1NF); NULL = unknown / unavailable / not applicable, two NULLs are not equal; closed world: a fact not in the state is false.

    Constraints

    • Three categories: inherent model-based (no duplicate tuples, atomic, unordered); schema-based in DDL (domain, key, NOT NULL, entity and referential integrity); application-based (business rules, via programs, assertions, triggers). Domain: each value atomic, from dom(A)\mathrm{dom}(A)dom(A).
    • Superkey: no two distinct tuples agree on it in any valid state; all attributes always one.
    • Key (candidate): minimal superkey (uniqueness + minimality). Single-attribute superkey is a key.
    • Primary key: the chosen candidate key, underlined, used by FKs; others are unique keys. Key = property of the schema (meaning), not of today’s data: Name is not a key.
    • Keys from a state: singles (a repeat kills it) →\to→ pairs →\to→ triples; keep minimal unique sets; data can only refute a key, so state the semantic assumption for the PK.
    • Superkey count: one key of kkk attrs: 2n−k2^{n-k}2n−k; two keys: 2n−∣K1∣+2n−∣K2∣−2n−∣K1∪K2∣2^{n-|K_1|}+2^{n-|K_2|}-2^{n-|K_1\cup K_2|}2n−∣K1​∣+2n−∣K2​∣−2n−∣K1​∪K2​∣; kkk single-attribute keys: (2k−1) 2n−k(2^k-1)\,2^{n-k}(2k−1)2n−k. E.g. keys {A,B},{C} in n=5n=5n=5: 8+16−4=208+16-4=208+16−4=20.
    • Entity integrity: no PK value (or part of one) is NULL; PK is implicitly NOT NULL.
    • Referential integrity / FK: FK of R1R_1R1​ has the domain of PK of R2R_2R2​, and each t1[FK]t_1[FK]t1​[FK] equals some t2[PK]t_2[PK]t2​[PK] or is NULL. May reference its own relation (Super_ssn); may be NULL unless NOT NULL or part of the PK; a composite FK references the whole composite PK.
    • Other: semantic; state (static) vs transition (“salary only increases”).

    Update operations: which constraint, which options

    OpDomKeyEIRIOptions
    Insert✓✓✓✓reject, or correct the cause
    Delete–––✓restrict, cascade, set null, set default
    Update non-key✓–––reject
    Update FK✓✓✓✓reject, or correct
    Update PK✓✓✓✓as Delete (ON UPDATE …)

    * only if the FK is part of the PK. Correct = valid value, FK NULL, or insert the referenced tuple first.

    • Insert RI: only on the referencing side (new FK dangles). Insert into a relation with no FK cannot break RI. A NULL FK is fine unless NOT NULL.
    • Delete: breaks only RI (deleted tuple is referenced). Options can be mixed: cascade into WORKS_ON, set null on Super_ssn.
    • Set null illegal when the FK is part of the referencing PK (WORKS_ON.Essn, DEPENDENT.Essn).
    • Update PK = delete + insert: key (duplicate), EI (NULL), RI (old value referenced).
    • List all violations: one insert can break domain and RI, or key and RI.
    • Populate-to-show-violations: valid tuples first, then one bad tuple per constraint, named.
    • Transaction: atomic group of operations, valid at the end. Joins: FK = PK equijoins rebuild relationships; other joins give spurious tuples.

    ER-to-relational mapping, Steps 1–7

    • 1 Strong entity: relation with all simple attributes (composite →\to→ its components); PK = one key, other keys UNIQUE; derived not stored.
    • 2 Weak entity: relation with its attributes + owner’s PK as FK; PK = owner PK + partial key; no relation for the identifying relationship; map a weak owner first; CASCADE.
    • 3 Binary 1:1: (a) FK approach (preferred): FK in the total side, UNIQUE (+ NOT NULL if total), relationship attributes there; (b) merge if both sides total; (c) cross-reference relation, PK one FK, other UNIQUE (few participants).
    • 4 Binary 1:N: FK in the N-side relation to the 1-side PK, plus relationship attributes; NOT NULL if N side total. Alternative: relationship relation keyed by the N-side PK (few participants).
    • 5 Binary M:N: new relation, both PKs as FKs, PK = their combination, plus attributes. No other option in 1NF (an FK holds one value).
    • 6 Multivalued attribute: new relation (A, owner PK K), PK = {A, K}; composite A: its components.
    • 7 nnn-ary: new relation with all nnn PKs as FKs + attributes; PK = all FKs, except a participant marked 1 drops out of the PK.
    • Not enforceable by FKs: total participation of the 1-side or of an M:N side, (min,max) bounds: state them (assertion, trigger, application).
    • Correspondence: entity →\to→ relation; 1:1/1:N →\to→ FK; M:N, nnn-ary →\to→ relation + FKs; composite →\to→ components; multivalued →\to→ relation + FK; value set →\to→ domain; key →\to→ PK/unique.

    EER mapping: Step 8 (specialization) and 9 (category)

    • 8A super + subs: L(k,super attrs)L(k,\text{super attrs})L(k,super attrs), each Li(k,own attrs)L_i(k,\text{own attrs})Li​(k,own attrs) with k→Lk\to Lk→L. Valid for every specialization; needs joins.
    • 8B subs only: each Li(k,super attrs,own attrs)L_i(k,\text{super attrs},\text{own attrs})Li​(k,super attrs,own attrs), no LLL. Only if total (else entities lost); recommended only if disjoint (overlap stores inherited data twice).
    • 8C one table, type ttt: L(k,all attrs,t)L(k,\text{all attrs},t)L(k,all attrs,t). Only disjoint; ttt NULL if partial, NOT NULL enforces total; attribute-defined: ttt = defining attribute. Many NULLs.
    • 8D one table, flags t1..tmt_1..t_mt1​..tm​: Boolean per subclass. For overlapping (works for disjoint); NULLs.
    • Lattices / hierarchies: mix options per level; a shared subclass may use any valid option.
    • 9 Category, different keys: category relation with a new surrogate key (Owner_id) + own attributes; surrogate as FK (UNIQUE, NULLable) in each superclass relation; type attribute recommended. Same key (CAR ∪\cup∪ TRUCK on Vehicle_id): no surrogate, use that key.

    Grading checklist (EtoR-I / GA3)

    • Major: relation with no PK / entity not mapped; weak PK without the owner’s full key; FK to part of a composite key; 1:N unmapped or FK on the 1-side; M:N not a relation or PK missing a key; ternary as binary or PK missing a participant; multivalued kept as a column; relationship attribute in the wrong relation; specialization lost (8C for overlapping); a diamond not mapped at all; no FK arrows.
    • Minor: one FK arrow missing/reversed; a PK attribute not underlined; composite kept whole; derived stored unmarked; identifying relationship as extra relation; no NOT NULL for total; no UNIQUE on 1:1 FK; an attribute missing; no explanation/assumptions.
    • Grades: A = 0 major, ≤2\le2≤2 minor; B = 1 major or ≥3\ge3≥3 minor; C = 2–3 major; D = ≥4\ge4≥4 major. Each occurrence counts; one wrong key carried consistently counts once. Justified alternatives accepted; names do not matter.

    Traps that cost marks

    • Delete violating key/EI, or RI on an insert into a relation with no FK: wrong.
    • Set null on a PK-part FK; forgetting NULL FKs are allowed; stopping at the first violation.
    • Each operation on the original state, not after earlier ones; name the offending value (“Dnum = 2 has no DEPARTMENT”) and the legal options.
    • “Key = primary key”: a relation can have several candidate keys; give a superkey that is not a key.
    • Weak entity keyed alone (BANK_BRANCH by Branch_no) ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ every FK to it is half a key (M2 + M3).
    • M:N folded into an entity (A_C into ACCOUNT); FK on the 1-side; Grade not in TAKES.
    • 8C for overlapping (a person who acts and directs); 8B for partial.
    • Missing NOT NULL on total N-side FKs and UNIQUE on 1:1 FKs (Dean_id, Mgr_ssn).

    Exam moves (mapping answer template)

    • 1. Assumptions A1, A2, …, each with a why: keys, how a ternary’s 1s are read, which Step 8 option and why.
    • 2. Step by step: Step 1 … Step 9, naming the construct handled in each.
    • 3. Final schema: one line per relation, PK underlined, every FK as A → R.B; NOT NULL for total, UNIQUE for 1:1; composite FKs as a group: (Title, Year) → TV_SHOW.
    • 4. Schema diagram: an arrow from every FK to the PK it references.
    • 5. Unenforceable constraints in one sentence (min >1>1>1, total on the 1-side). Violation questions: operation, constraint(s), offending value, options.
